utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE

After receiving the evidence this morning and perhaps tomorrow afternoon, the Chamber will adjourn and review the evidence and then make a determination as to whether or not reasonable grounds, that is, prima facie evidence, has been offered with respect to the indictment. We expect that we will issue that decision on or about May 2nd. Are you ready to proceed, Mr. Cayley, or who will begin first?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very well. You may proceed, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, we have filed this morning an application, your Honour, requesting that when we arrive to listen to the first witness, we would ask you to grant an order that the names, addresses, whereabouts and other identifying information concerning persons previously identified by pseudonym, witnesses A, B, C, D, E, F and G, should not be disclosed to the media or to the public; that the names, addresses, whereabouts and other identifying information concerning witnesses A to G should be sealed and not included in any of the Tribunal's public records; that the pseudonym witnesses A to G should be used whenever referring to these witnesses in Tribunal proceedings and that any discussions relative to the issue of protective measures for pseudonym witnesses should be heard in closed sessions. I will go on reading this motion. On 29th August 1995, the indictment against Ivica Rajic was confirmed by Judge Rustam Sidhwa. Subsequently, on March 6th 1996, upon considering an application by the Prosecutor, Judge Sidhwa ordered pursuant to Rule 61A that the indictment against Ivica Rajic be submitted to the Trial Chamber for proceedings commencing on this day, today. They were rescheduled to 1st April and then scheduled to the date of today. After confirmation of the indictment, statements were taken from survivors of the attack on Stupni Do by Tribunal investigators. At the time their statements were taken those witnesses agreed to testify before the Tribunal. However, for purposes of the proceedings, the Tribunal's investigator who recorded their statements will give oral testimony as to their evidence. It has not been possible to consult with the witness A to witness G prior to these proceedings and there are serious concerns which exist in relation to their security.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I received that motion this morning and I have reviewed it and conferred with my fellow judges and we have granted that motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, your Honour, I will proceed with my opening statements.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The indictment we submit to the Trial Chamber today deals with the attack by Bosnia Croat soldiers belonging to the Croatian Defence Council, which I will refer to as the HVO, on the Muslim inhabited village of Stupni Do in central Bosnia. A map, your Honour, of central Bosnia will be on the screens before all of you in the courtroom. Sometimes when I refer to places, they can be identified and they will be put up before you so you can see with a little arrow exactly what I am talking about. For this attack Ivica Rajic, then the Commander of the HVO forces in Vares, approximately four kilometres north west of Stupni Do, is charged under Article 7(1) in three separate counts, firstly and secondly, with Grave Breaches of the Geneva Conventions, punishable under Article 2(a) and (d) of the Statute as wilful killing and destruction of property; thirdly, with violations of the Laws or Customs of War, punishable under Article 3 of the Statute as a deliberate attack on the civilian population and wanton destruction of the village. Alternatively to each count, Ivica Rajic is charged under Article 7 paragraph 3 of the Statute with failure, in his superior authority, to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the attacks and to punish the perpetrators of it. To put this attack in an understandable context, I will start with giving a short overview of the political and military circumstances in which the attack took place. These circumstances are in more detail set out in the brief I submitted to the Trial Chamber yesterday. It is, of course, impossible in the context of an opening statement in a Rule 61 Hearing to give a full and detailed background to the fact that an armed conflict erupted between the Bosnian Croat and the Muslims in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993. In more detail again this will be set out in our brief. Some outlining facts, however, might serve the purpose of facilitating the understanding. Bosnia and Herzegovina declared itself independent on 6th March 1992. On April 6th 1992, the European Community recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina and the following day it was recognised by the United States and by Croatia. Croatia immediately offered all Bosnian Croats dual citizenship with Croatia. However, prior to the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, on 18th November 1991, a Croatian community in Bosnia-Herzegovina was established. They called themselves the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, thereby emphasising the Herzegovine region which has throughout history been the centre of Croatian nationalism in Bosnia. In the declaration establishing the Croatian Community in Bosnia-Herzegovina, specific municipalities in Bosnia were designated as falling within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, amongst them is Vares, the municipality in which Stupni Do is located. Although predominantly Croatian, this area incorporated towns and villages where Muslims formed a majority. When the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992, the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims were united in defending Bosnia and Herzegovina against aggression coming from Bosnian Serbs and from the National Yugoslavian Army. They even entered a formal military alliance against the Serbian and Yugoslav forces. However, as early as May 1992 there were tensions between the Bosnian Croats and the Muslims in that alliance, when the Yugoslavian National Army was officially pulling out of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which happened in May 1992. They were starting to quarrel over the question of who would get the arms and the munitions that this Army had left behind it. Signs of conflict could also be seen later in 1992 on questions relating to arms. When the Vance-Owen plan, which attributed certain areas to respective parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was announced the conflict between the former allies escalated. An April 16th 1993, HVO forces attacked the predominantly Muslim village of Ahmici, also in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina and summarily executed scores of unarmed civilians and destroyed the Muslim homes. That attack has resulted in another indictment at this Tribunal. On May 9th 1993, the HVO started an attack in Mostar, that had been made the capital of the self-declared Croation Community of Herceg-Bosna, where thousands of Muslims, men, women and children were arbitrarily arrested by the HVO. The next remarkable event in the armed conflict between the two parties is the attack on Stupni Do, resulting in the indictment which we submit today under Rule 61 of our Statute. Let us now have a look on the maps before you. Stupni Do is located in the municipality of Vares, some four kilometres southeast of the city of Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Some four kilometres southeast of the city of Vares. It was a small town -- I use the past tense because, as you will see from the photos we are going to present, it is totally devastated and no longer inhabitable -- it was a city or village of about 250 people living in some 60 houses. The population consisted mostly of workers having some farm land and cattle. The inhabitants regarded themselves as a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Stupni Do was a typical country village. There were no military installations whatsoever. It is situated somewhat off the main road and several witnesses who were senior army officers of the UNPROFOR -- that is the United Nations protection forces -- have stated that it was of no military interest to any of the parties. In October 1993 the HVO controlled the municipality of Vares and had the military authority in the area through the Bobovac Brigade, with headquarters based three kilometres north east of Vares near Ponikva. Can we also see Ponikva? In October 1993 the Bobovac Brigade came under the command of the Second Operational Group of the HVO, based in Kiseljak approximately 30 kilometres southeast of Vares. The commander of that group in October 1993 was Ivica Rajic, known to previously have been a first class captain of the Yugoslavian Army. On or about 21st October 1993, Rajic came to Vares with a large number of troops from the Kiseljak area. The Brigade Commander was removed and Rajic took military control of Vares and the Bobovac Brigade. We will bring two witnesses to the fact that Rajic was the commander, namely, Brigadier-General Ulf Henricsson, Commanding Officer of Nordic Battalion of the United Nations Protection Force, and his interpreter and Assistant, Ruzdi Ekenheim, who will tell you that Rajic acted and represented himself as the officer in command of the HVO in Vares and Stupni Do and specifically as the Brigade Commander. Lieutenant Colonel Jan Koet, a Dutch Legal Officer of the UNPROFOR, will tell you that it was later confirmed by the HVO that Rajic was the commander responsible for troops attacking Stupni Do. Under the command of Ivica Rajic, there were approximately 200 HVO soldiers. At about 8 o'clock in the morning of October 23rd 1993, these soldiers attacked the village with unspecified fire and then entered the village, went from house to house, took money and possessions, killed or forced inhabitants to flee and set the houses on fire. One of our investigators, Ehsan Bajwa, which will be our first witness today, will summarise the statements of victims and eyewitnesses. The British Navy photographer, Bernard Pettersen, then serving with the UNPROFOR, will show you pictures taken by him in the village after the attack. All this will show that what happened to Stupni Do was an illegal attack on the civilian population of the village with the sole purpose to terrorise, kill and drive away the Muslim population. These are the facts I present in my opening statement. I will now turn to some legal questions of applicable law pertaining to this indictment. Ivica Rajic is charged with responsibility for committing Grave Breaches of the Geneva Conventions contrary to Article 2 of the Statute, and with responsibility for a deliberate attack on the civilian population and wanton destruction of the village of Stupni Do contrary to Article 3 of the Statute. The Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal has held in its decision on Defence Motion for the Interlocutory Appeal on Jurisdiction in the case of Prosecutor v. Tadic, I quote, that "Article 2 of the Statute only applies to offences committed within the context of international armed conflicts". With reference to counts I, II, IV and V, it is the submission of the Prosecution that in October 1993 an international armed conflict existed between Bosnia and Croatia, that HVO forces under the command of Ivica Rajic were under the control of Croatia in this conflict to such an extent that they must be regarded as agents and, in the words of the Appeals Chamber's decision, paragraph 76, "acting not as a rebellious entity but as organs or agents of another State". The Prosecution also submits that the persons and property in the village of Stupni Do were protected within the meaning of the Fourth Geneva Convention on the protection of civilians, vis-a-vis Croatia controlled forces. The fourth Geneva Convention applies during any international armed conflict between two or more of the High Contracting Parties. Both Bosnia and Croatia were parties to all of the Geneva Conventions and they were engaged in an armed conflict with each other when the attack on Stupni Do occurred. Croatia acceded to the four Geneva Conventions and the Two Additional Protocols on May 11th 1992 and Bosnia and Herzegovina acceded to the four Geneva Conventions and the same Two Additional Protocols on 31st December 1992. Protected persons under the Fourth Geneva Convention are, and I quote from Article 4: "Those who, at a given moment and in any manner whatsoever, find themselves, in case of a conflict or occupation, in the hands of a Party to the conflict or Occupying Power of which they are not nationals". Real or personal property is protected from destruction in occupied territory except where such destruction is rendered absolutely necessary by military operations. Under Article 147 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, Grave Breaches include wilful killing of protected persons and the extensive destruction of property, not justified by military necessity and carried out unlawfully and wantonly. It is the submission of prosecution that, once Stupni Do was overrun by HVO forces under the command of Ivica Rajic, Stupni Do became occupied territory and Croatia became the occupying power. The inhabitants of Stupni Do were Bosnian nationals and the real and personal property of Stupni Do was Bosnian property. The fact that Ivica Rajic and the HVO forces under his command might also be regarded as Bosnian nationals is legally irrelevant because the degree of control exercised by Croatia over the self-proclaimed Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO was so great that this entity must be regarded as agents or extensions of Croatia. The killings of civilians and the destruction of property which occurred in Stupni Do once the village was overrun constitute, therefore, Grave Breaches of the Geneva Conventions. With reference to counts II, III, V and VI, it is the submission of the Prosecutor that the alleged attack against the civilian population and wanton destruction of the village of Stupni Do are prohibited under international customary and conventional law, in both international and internal conflicts. These counts refer to acts which occurred during the attack. In the Decision on Jurisdiction, the Appeals Chamber held, in paragraph 127 that with respect to all armed conflicts, customary law "covers such areas as protection of civilian objects, in particular from indiscriminate attacks, protection of civilian objects, in particular cultural property, protection of all those who do not (or no longer) take active part in hostilities, as well as prohibition of means of warfare conducting hostilities". The arguments on applicable law are set out more fully in the same brief submitted to the Trial Chamber yesterday. Your Honour, with these observations I conclude my opening statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I suppose it should be made clear that this does not result in an adjudication of guilt or innocence. What this is is an opportunity for the Prosecutor to present in open court the indictment, as I indicated, that was confirmed by Judge Sidhwa as well as offer additional evidence and, particularly, the testimony of witnesses. At the conclusion of the receipt of that evidence, then it is the responsibility of the judges to make a determination as to whether or not there are reasonable grounds to support the charges that have been made in the indictment against the accused. If, however, the Chamber finds that there are reasonable grounds, that does not mean that there is an adjudication of guilt. The accused has been indicted and, of course, should he choose to surrender to the Tribunal, then he would be entitled to a trial and the trial would be conducted in his presence. So this is not a trial in absentia; it is merely an opportunity for the Prosecutor to present this evidence. If the Tribunal or if the Trial Chamber makes a determination that there are reasonable grounds, that is, a prime facie case has been established, then the Trial Chamber may issue an international arrest warrant for the arrest of the accused. If the Chamber finds that the failure to execute the arrest warrant is because of a lack of co-operation on the part of the State to whom the arrest warrant was directed, then the Trial Chamber may ask the President of the Tribunal to advise the Security Council of this lack of co-operation. So I really wanted to put the proceedings in context and make it very clear what we are doing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We are in total agreement, your Honour. But I think I would take the advantage of this opportunity to say now that we are not invoking paragraph (E) of the Rule 61 which tells us: "If the Prosecutor satisfies the Trial Chamber that the failure to effect personal service was due in whole or in part to a failure or refusal of a State to co-operate with the Tribunal in accordance", etc., the Trial Chamber can, as your Honour pointed out, ask the President to notify the Security Council. We are not in the position to satisfy ourselves or your Honours that this was a failure of any special state or any special entity, because we believe that there are political and practical, military or other circumstances who can have made it impossible to execute the warrants. Therefore, I am not trying, in this case, to satisfy the Trial Chamber that it was the failure of any specific State.

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: -- they are not to be treated as witnesses or what are they -- in this list?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the first bundle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Interviews with so and so -----

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is simply written evidence, your Honour, that is being submitted. May I proceed with the witness, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: The second bundle is page 497 where we have camouflaged their identity and refer to as A, B, C, D, E, F and G?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: All right. Page 497, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Cayley, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Examined by MR. CAYLEY

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are Mr. Ehsan Bajwa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it is correct, is it not, that you are a superintendent in the Police Force in Pakistan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you have now been a senior Police Officer in Pakistan for a period of seven years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you were very kindly given a leave of absence in September '95 by your Police Force so that you could serve as an investigator with this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think since your arrival at the Tribunal you have spent a number of months in Bosnia-Herzegovina taking statements from Bosnian nationals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you have been particularly concerned with interviewing a number of survivors from the attack on the village of Stupni Do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you conducted in all seven statements; is that correct? You conducted seven interviews with witnesses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from these seven statements, there are some other statements, but in so far as the ocular account of what happened, these are the seven statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think in each case the interview that you conducted with this witness was conducted through a certified interpreter who is fluent in both English and Bosnian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you addressed your questions to the witness in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the interpreter then interpreted your request to the witness into Bosnian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I think that the response of the witness was given, of course, back by the witness to you in Bosnian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think then the interpreter interpreted that response for your benefit into English; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, indeed, it is correct that you made a written record of the witness's interpreted response; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I think is it true that the entire English record of that statement was read back to the witness in Bosnian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I think that any matter with which the witness disagreed or was uncertain was, in fact, corrected by you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I think only when the witness was fully satisfied with the statement did he or she sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bajwa. If I could produce Prosecutor's Exhibit 1, if this could be handed to the witness, please? (Handed) Could you just not open it for a moment, Mr. Bajwa? There are a couple of questions I would like to ask you first. I think on 18th March 1996 you interviewed witness A; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you requested of witness A what his function was in the village of Stupni Do. Can you tell the court what he said to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness described himself as the President of the local community of Stupni Do and, by virtue of that position in the community of Stupni Do, he recalled that he was responsible for co-ordinating with the municipal authorities of Vares in such public affairs and matters as roads in the village and telephones in the village, electricity in the village, educational facilities and health facilities. So he was a man who was actively involved with the public affairs at the local level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you showed that witness a photograph, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think is that the photograph that is in front of you at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That will become Prosecutor's Exhibit 1. We tender that in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that going to appear on our monitor?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Portions of it, your Honour, are going to appear; the entire photograph will not. Mr. Bajwa will refer to the photographic copy next to him and, indeed, a more focused image of that map, of that photograph, will come up in front of you. I think it will become quite clear to you as his testimony unfolds.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So this was a photograph which he used when he was questioning witness A?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you know where this photograph came from? Who took it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It is, in fact, an aerial photographer. In fact, I will ask the witness. (To the witness): Do you know where this photograph came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My impression of the photograph is that it is an aerial photograph of the village of Stupni Do and, indeed, it was recognised as such by witness A, and in so far as this is the sour of the aerial photograph is concerned, my impression it was lent by a friendly government.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's Exhibit 1 then will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. (To the witness): I think the witness assisted you, did he not, by identifying buildings, topographical features and cultural sites within the village from this aerial photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that, indeed, you and he together marked those features on this aerial photograph with yellow markers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, yellow stickers, paper stickers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think he then made a statement identifying each of those marked features; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the statement is, as it were, a key to the aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a statement -- all these marks on the photograph are to be read in conjunction with the statement for understanding the significance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could in the course of your evidence, Mr. Bajwa, when you are referring to a particular witness whose place of residence has been identified on that photograph, if you could refer to it on the photograph and, indeed, so that the judges can understand from the screens in front of them exactly the area of the village that you are talking about, I would be grateful. Then you. If we could now, please, move to Witness B. I will lead you through a lot of your evidence, but there are some responses where I would like you to respond as you heard it from the witness when you took this statement. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B, I believe, was a woman who had lived in Stupni Do for almost 20 years prior to the attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, 20 years of her married life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she, indeed, had a husband and two children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she told you, did she not, that there were approximately 60 houses in the village, and that prior to the breakdown of the former Yugoslavia Stupni Do had to a degree been an ethnically mixed village; is that correct? If you would explain that in some detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ethnically mixed to the extent witness recorded that there were about 10 Serb houses in the village, and she had recorded there was no Croat house in the village of Stupni Do as such, except for the fact that there was one woman, a Croat woman, whether was married to a Muslim man in the village, so it was just one mixed family, mixed Croat Muslim family, and apart from that fact there were about 10 Serb houses in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think Witness B lived in a hamlet, a smaller area of the village, which was called Pricado; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you identify that on the map in front of you and also on the television screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not have the image here, but on this photograph it is the area which is marked as "A", and that is a hamlet of the whole village of Stupni Do which is at a point which is higher compared with the other portion of the village. So, it was relatively higher portion of the village which was referred to by the residents of Stupni Do as Pricado.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think your Honours you, indeed, have that portion of the aerial photograph on the screens in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, we have, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: MR. CAYLEY (To the witness): Could you say which number her house was on this aerial photograph, the house in which she resided at the time of the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was No. 5. It is No. 5 here. It was a comparatively bigger building in the hamlet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the witness explained to you, did she not, that the HVO authorities in Vares gradually began to exert more and more pressure on the village of Stupni Do after they, in fact, ceased power in the town in June 1992. I wondered if you could briefly tell a little bit about what she said to you to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Witness B recalled that women from Muslim villages like Stupni Do and Strijezevo -- and these are the villages which were within the municipality of Vares, but which were situated at a certain distance from the town of Vares -- those women would go to town to sell their country merchandise, like cheese, butter, eggs, vegetables, and the fact that they were of Muslim ethnicity could be determined by what they were wearing. They could be marked for that. She recalled that the name of the dress was "dimija". She explained that "demija" is like a skirt which comes down, close down, up to the feet and it is a baggy dress. So, whenever there was a Muslim woman from a certain Muslim village, it could easily be detected that she is of Muslim ethnicity. She recalled that such women were harassed while they were on their tours to the town to sell or to buy things, and Croats, there were frequent incidents of them being intimidated, they being told not to come to the town and if they had to come at all they should not be wearing dimijas. That was one aspect of the harassment that she spoke of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she also told you, in fact, about a kidnapping that occurred just shortly before the attack on Stupni Do; I wonder if you could tell the court about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is as far as the women were concerned, but in so far as men were concerned, the witness recalled that lots of times there were events when men would be taken to a certain building in the town of Vares. They will be asked what their names are. Those names will be taken down. Some of them would be held in detention for a certain number of days and then, after being robbed of whatever possessions they had, they would be let off. At other times, they would be indefinitely detained. She exactly and specifically recalled one such incident about a week before the actual attack that took place on 23rd October 1993. In that incident she recalled that six men, and she was very specific about their names as well, those six men were travelling on a certain unbeaten, far flung country road because they wanted to avoid being arrested, but still they could not avoid it. They were intercepted and they were arrested. They could not escape unless -- the municipality of Vares was taken by the Bosnian Army in November and it is only after the take-over by Bosnian Army that they were able to escape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me get this clear; eight days prior to the attack on Stupni Do, a group of men from the village were, as it were, arrested and taken away whilst travelling from Stupni Do to another village nearby; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were travelling towards Stupni Do from a neighbouring village, and she recalled the name of the village they were travelling from to Stupni Do was Budozelj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, these same men were not released until sometime after the attack on Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, and they had their tales of beatings and tortures to tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this witness said something to you about the village guard force in Stupni Do. I wondered if you could tell the court a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that there were about 20 men who composed the local village guard, and she said that none of those men was from outside the village of Stupni Do. All of them were native residents of the village of Stupni Do. Then she recalled that not all of them had uniforms and even those who did not have full uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these men were not, in fact, regular members of the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She did not put it that way, but she said that they were just local guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. If we can actually now move forward to the attack itself. At what time and date did the witness say that the attack took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the witness recalled that it was on 23rd October 1993 at about 10 minutes past 8 with the explosion of a shell the attack started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the witness do when the attack started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that the witness -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was that a.m. or p.m.?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is a.m., your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Witness B recalled that they were a family of four in their house, No. 5, in the hamlet of Pricado, and this family of four consisted of witness herself, her husband, her 17 year old daughter and 15 year old son. She recalled that that morning, that Saturday morning, on 23rd October, she was taking breakfast with her son and with her daughter, and there was the sudden explosion of a shell. Hearing that explosion, she rushed to the door of the house to see what was happening outside, and she recalled that it was as if the explosion of the shell announced a certain kind of a start, because it was immediately followed with intense firing and, as she was out of her house, she saw that bullets were coming from all sides, from all the different directions. Then she recalled that when she was out of her house she saw this boy who was about 12 years of age, she knew him to be from the village, and he was standing nearby her house tending his cows and standing by the cows. The boy was crying and she asked him to come over and to rush for his life. The boy said that, "What am I going to do with my cows?" She told him just to rush and forget about cows. So, the boy came over and with the arrival of the boy in Witness B's house, the number of people in the house became five, two children of the witness and her husband and with this boy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the small boy. I think these five people, the family of Witness B and this small boy, waited in the bathroom of the house, they took shelter in their bathroom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that by the time she came back the windows and the glass panes in the windows were all broken because bullets had struck them. She did not know where to go. So she went to the bathroom with all her family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at that stage they were, in fact, joined by others, is that correct, or in fact they went and joined others because the house in which they lived was occupied by two families; is that correct? Could you explain that to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was actually a bigger building, and the witness recalled that the building housed two families and the neighbouring family consisted of three people at that time at the start of the attack. Presently, after spending about an hour inside the bathroom, they went to the neighbouring family and both of them decided that they should go to a shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, indeed, it is true, is it not, that this group of eight people decided that they would go to a sturdier shelter in another part of the village. In fact, I think they went to Witness A's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the court which number marked on the aerial photograph is Witness A's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is No. 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So No. 1, your Honours, on the screens in front of you indicates the house to which this group of eight people fled just after the beginning of the attack. (To the witness): The next part of the witness's testimony is very important, so I would like you to tell it to the court in the words which the witness used to you because I understand at this stage all of these people were, in fact, hiding in the basement of witness A's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, if you would tell the court in your own words what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that when they reached the shelter in the basement of witness A's house, she found that there were already 10 people who were sheltered in that basement, which of course included witness A's family also. Together with those 10 people and these eight people from house five, they became 18 totally in the numbers. Amongst these 18 people there were three men and five women and the rest were children. So she recalled that the firing continued and after a certain length of time her husband said: "I will go out and see what is happening outside". So the husband went out with another man and came back, and all of these 18 people were hiding in a back room in the basement. She remembered that she heard her husband speaking to the other men and saying that the defences of village have fallen and they are almost on the verge of entering the village. Then she recalled that everybody wanted to flee the basement in which they were hiding, but only three of them were able to escape and the rest were left behind, which means about the number of people that were left behind were 15 in the shelter. Three were able to escape immediately before the arrival of the attacking soldiers in this specific building in the basement. Then she recalled that when those three people had escaped, she with everybody else, she heard sound of footsteps on the stairs that went up to the upper floor of the same building in whose basement they were hiding. Then she recalled that those same sounds, the stomp of boots, started coming from the ceiling and then she recalled that there was lots of sounds of firing from the upper floor, and it was as if all the windows are being broken and everything is being thrown around. Then presently she recalled a certain girl who also lived in the same neighbourhood, and who she thought might have been discovered hiding somewhere, hidden somewhere, by the attacking troops. She remembered that while hidden in that basement she heard the voice of that neighbouring girl who was 17 years of age approximately at that time. The voice was saying: "Come out. They know that you are hiding here". Then she recalled that after that voice two soldiers entered the basement in which these 15 people, after the departure and escape of three people, were hidden. Then she recalled that she was very -- she gave a very vivid account of how those two soldiers looked. She recalled that their eyes were bloodshot and they were wearing camouflage uniforms and she described their faces as "beastly" faces. That is what she literally said. Then she recalled that all of them were ordered out of where these 15 people were hiding. She recalled that as she was moving out of the basement one of the soldiers grabbed her daughter, her 17-year old daughter, who was also hidden in the same shelter with Witness B. That soldier grabbed the daughter by her arm saying: "Give me your beauty". Then she recalled that saying this, he started dragging the daughter away. She recalled that her daughter was screaming and she was struggling to pull away. That same soldier who was grabbing the daughter by her arm was joined by another soldier who started hitting her daughter with his rifle and kicking her in the back, and each time the daughter tried to pull away the other soldier who was assisting the first soldier would hit her in the back and push her in the back with the butt of his rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this point the daughter was taken to a house, was she not, by these two soldiers and then all the remaining people in the basement were driven out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, and the house that she was taken to, the witness specifically mentioned, was house No. 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: House No. 3. So that is where the daughter of Witness B was taken to by the two soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Cayley, before you continue, we will need to stand in recess for about five minutes, please. (Adjourned for a short time) (11.40 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. If I could just recap I think on what the witness had just said. I think he had just confirmed to me after I had put the question to him that the two soldiers then in fact drove the remaining civilians hiding in the basement of Witness A out of the basement to the outside. Could you just confirm that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think indeed at this stage the two soldiers who were outside who had taken this group of three men women and children outside separated the men from the women; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this stage the witness actually gave a description of the uniform that the soldiers were wearing, and I wondered if you could explain the description that she gave, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled they were wearing camouflage uniforms and they had white cloth ribbons tied around their uppers arms, and some of them had black bands tied around their heads and a few of them had crosses made of some shiny material hanging from their necks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. I think at this stage the soldiers began taking money and jewellery from these people they had brought outside; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the next events that took place, it would be best if you actually explain that in the words of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that as one of these soldiers was collecting money and the jewellery that the women were wearing, men were standing aside, they were not standing in the line, and one of the soldiers approached one of those three men that were there, and she recalled that the name of that man was Rifed. That soldier was standing behind Rifed and taking out a knife. He attacked Rifed and brought his arm over his shoulder right in front of his neck, and then pulled the knife across hitting Rifed at his neck just above the collar bone. She recalled that she saw blood streaming out and she saw Rifed bending over his knees, and the same soldier who had attacked Rifed with his knife lashed at the back of Rifed when he was bent over with his rifle and pushed him down on the ground and then he shot him dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there was then ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for one moment, if I may. Is this Witness B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Who told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think at this stage there was in fact another act of violence, and I wondered if you could tell the court in the words of the witness what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that after the murder of Rifed there were two men left in this group of 15 that had become 16 with the arrival of the neighbouring girl, and the witness recalled that one of those two men who were left was her husband Maho, as she recalled his name, and she recalled that Maho had already surrendered his money and he was holding out his wallet just to ensure the soldier that he has already given the money. The same soldier who had knifed and slit Rifed and shot him, shot him dead, told him to stretch himself flat on the ground and the witness recalled that her husband stretched himself flat on the ground, his face downwards, and the same soldier shot just below his left shoulder and her husband was dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the third man who was in this group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other two stretched themselves flat on the ground for both the men, and the third whose name was Edin and whose mother was also in the group standing in the line, he was also ordered to stretch himself flat on the ground. He stretched himself. He lay flat on the ground and he was also in a similar way shot dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there was indeed one further killing and if you could, again, explain to the court what happened in the words of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that they were standing in the line after these three men had been murdered. The woman who was standing first in the line on Witness B's left was by the name of Sida, and she recalled that when these three men were killed Sida wept out, questioning: "Why are you doing this to us? What harm have we done to you?" Witness B recalled that the same soldier struck Sida in her head with his boots. Sida fell down on the ground. She was in a prostrate position and she was crying: "Don't do this to me because my foot is hurting", and the same soldier said: "What do you mean your foot hurts?" Then he put his boots on the head of prostrate Sida and the witness recalled that there was a small tree stump on the ground, and he bent Sida's head on that tree stump and pinning her head in such a way he shot her dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this stage the remaining people were forced into a shed. Could you point out on the aerial photograph where that shed is located? I think it was actually specifically referred to as a summer kitchen, but it was in the nature of a shed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is No. 2 on this image.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there was some discussion amongst these HVO soldiers, which indeed the witness told you about, as to whether or not to shoot them or burn them alive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think indeed they were put into this shed, forced into this shed, and that that shed was then locked by an HVO soldier because the key was on the outside of the doors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the court in the words of the witness what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Witness B distinctly remembered that when she was being taken to what she called "summer house" she saw soldiers throwing two dead bodies. There were three men who had been killed and one woman, and she saw two dead bodies being thrown into a burning house which was at that instance house No. 3 here. That house had meanwhile been put on fire, and in this house she saw two dead bodies being thrown. The witness could not see whose dead bodies those were. So, on her way to seeing these two dead bodies being thrown, she went inside and all of them were locked up in the summer house. She eventually saw lots of smoke through the glass panes of the window of the summer house. There was lots of smoke, and after a while she saw that the glass of the windows was shattering and she also saw flames outside. She concluded that the summer house that they were confined into was on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think then at that point the witness explains to you that she uses an axe to break open the door; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I think the group that was remaining indeed escaped to the surrounding forest around Stupni Do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I think eventually they made their way to the village of Pajtov Han which is a nearby village to Stupni Do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where I think in fact they were arrested by local HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true. There was a checkpoint there and they were stopped there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think they were then rescued by members of the local United Nations Protection Force who took them to Breeza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if we could now move on to the next witness. Now this is Witness C. Are you familiar with Witness C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have an understanding of who Witness C is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness C I understand is the 19 year old son of Witness B; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19 year old now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of the attack on Stupni Do he would have been 16 years of age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that he was with his mother throughout all of the incidents that you have just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does he in fact corroborate his mother's account of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can deal with this witness very quickly, your Honours, because in fact he broadly corroborates what his mother says. So I do not think we need to go into any of the detail again. At what time does this witness believe that the attack commenced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was near 8 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he know that the attack had commenced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that there were three shell explosions and he went out of the house and he recalled that he saw houses on fire, and that is how he recalled the attacks started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does he state that the family immediately went to take shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He recalled that it was the bathroom of the house that they went into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whose basement shelter does he state that his family moved to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He recalled that it was the house of Witness A which is marked as No. 1 here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think he confirms, does he not, like his mother that a neighbouring girl comes to the basement with several HVO soldiers, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think he gives a description of the badge and the uniform that these soldiers were wearing. Could you describe that to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This witness seemed to have had a very clear impression of the shoulder badge that the soldiers were wearing. The witness recalled that they were wearing camouflage uniforms and on the shoulder badge he recalled that there were two rifles vertically placed, and he said that those were M-48 rifles. The background colour of the badge was green and amidst those two vertically placed rifles he recalled was a Croat checkerboard and at the top of the checkerboard were written the letters "HVO", and just beneath their butts, where the two buttons of the two rifles came together, he recalled were written in the form of curve, an arc, the words "Croatian Defence Council".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this is correct, is it not, that this witness confirms the death of the three men as described by Witness B; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I think this witness also in fact confirms that the remaining women and children were forced into the summer house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think he also confirms, does he not, that his mother breaks out of this summer house, or breaks open the door to the summer house, with an axe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I then think he states or stated to you that he escaped with the other survivors to the local woods; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think he also confirmed to you that, like his mother, he escaped to Pajtov Han where at an HVO checkpoint he was taken into custody by the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think he gives more detail than his mother about the arrival of UN Protection Force. Could you tell the court something about what he said about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that they were stopped at an HVO checkpoint which was located in the village of Pajtov Han, and he also remembered the name of the soldiers who were manning that HVO checkpoint, and he recalled that both of those soldiers were residents of Vares and he knew them. He recalls that about half an hour after they had been stopped at that checkpoint two UNPROFOR trucks came, and he recalled that he knew that in Vares the UNPROFOR troops are from Sweden. He recalled that those trucks came near them and stopped nearby them, and two soldiers, UNPROFOR soldiers, came out of those trucks. He recalled that one of those soldiers was speaking Bosnian language, and he came up to them, the Bosnian language speaking UNPROFOR soldier, and he asked them who they were and where they wanted to go. Then the same soldier, UNPROFOR soldier who was speaking Bosnian language, he went up to the two HVO soldiers who were manning that checkpoint and asked them, "Why don't you let them off? Why don't you release them? Why are they standing here?" And the soldier who the Witness C recognises and remembers his name, said that, "We can only give them permission to go with the prior permission of Ivica Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically the witness said to you with the prior permission of Ivica Rajic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think indeed the UN Protection Force truck left after this had been said to them, and then returned approximately half an hour later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I think at that stage all of the remaining survivors were take to Dabravine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this witness also says something about the total number of dead from Stupni Do, and I wondered if you could very briefly summarise to the court what the witness said to you and how he actually supported his assertions about the final number of dead, the final number of dead in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that one week after his after he had been rescued and taken Dabravine, UNPROFOR brought the remains of 16 natives of Stupni Do and he was there in Breeza and he saw the remains of those 16 natives of Stupni Do who had been, who had died during the October 1993 attack. Then he recalled that after Rajic was taken by Bosnian Army in November 1993, and he recalled that it was his birthday somewhere in November 1993, when he accompanied the new troops to the village of Stupni Do to assist them with their efforts to search for the remains of some other natives of Stupni Do who died during the attack, and he said that he personally saw the remains of six other people being recovered. He specifically gave the names of those six other natives of Stupni Do who died during the October 1993 attack. Apart from these 16 and six people, he said that he knew that there were 16 other people who died during the attack, and he heard from others who also assisted with the search for the bodies, he heard it being said from them and he also specified the locations that he heard being mentioned in connection with the remains of those bodies. But he said that he did not see them being found out; he only heard about them from others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much indeed. If we could move on to the next witness, your Honours, which is in fact Witness D. Mr. Bajwa, are you familiar with the identity of Witness B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And familiar with the testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think Witness D is a 35 year old woman who in fact was married to the President of the Community, Witness A; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think Witness A had two children at the time of the attack aged 10 and 6; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think again this witness was present during the same events as Witnesses B and C. So, if you can just confirm, as it were, corroboration of what they had said I think that will be adequate for the purposes of the court rather than repeating all the evidence again. I think that this witness actually said something quite interesting about the village Guard Force in Stupni Do, and I wonder if you could briefly state to the court what she said about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Witness D recalled that the number of people in the village guard was about 30 to 40, and she said that they were all men who were natives of Stupni Do. She said none of them was from outside the village of Stupni Do, except for one exception that she made. She said that there was one soldier, and she also gave his name, who was visiting his brother at the time of the attack who also might have been involved in defending the village at the time of the attack, but otherwise it was a Guard Force that was composed exclusively of the natives of Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this witness confirms, does she not, that the attack commenced at 8 o'clock in the morning of 23rd October 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She also states, does she not, that she perceived that the attack had commenced because she had heard shooting from all around; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she then stated to you that she ran to the shelter in the basement of the house with her two children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she also confirmed to you the arrival of Witnesses B and C into the basement shelter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She also confirms the death of the three men which you have explained through the evidence of Witness B. She says something quite interesting and it is certainly relevant for the purpose of these proceedings about these three men. Can you say to the court what she said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She recalled that all three of them had impediments. She talked about Rifed, the first man who was murdered, and she recalled that Rifed had a congenital deformity in his foot, and about Edin who also happened to be her brother-in-law, a brother of her husband, she recalled that he had some nervous problem. He had some kind of a mental impediment. Concerning Mehmo, the third man who was murdered in Pricado, she recalled that he had had some kind of a spinal fracture at his workplace. So all three of them were handicapped in different ways. She also mentioned the dresses, civilian clothes, that all three of them were wearing at the time when they were found in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think she also says something, does she not, about the appearance of the soldiers who came to the basement and something about their uniforms. I wondered if you could tell the court what she said about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that the attacking soldiers were clad in camouflage uniforms, and she recalled that some of them had their faces plastered with camouflage paint, and some of them were wearing gloves without fingers, fingerless gloves, and she recalled that they were armed with rifles and with knives and some of those knives were in the sheaths that were hanging from their belts, and some of those knives were tucked in their boots that they were wearing. She also had a clear memory of the shoulder badges that they were wearing, and she recalled that the design of the shoulder badge was such that there was a big "U" and inside the two arms of the "U" was a Croat checkerboard, red and white, and at the top of the two arms of the U were written letters "HVO" and she recalled that just beneath the "U" were some roses and some branches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, as I have just stated, she confirms the death of the three men who were present at the time. She also says something about her young son. Could you explain to the court what she says about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the witness recalled that after the murder of Rifed, the same soldier was holding the same knife that he had killed Rifed with, and he brought that knife to her son that was standing, and she was holding the hand of her son, her two sons, and the soldier put the blade of the knife just underneath the chin of the son, just on his throat, and when he was doing it and she had a clear impression that the soldier was about to slit the throat of her son, and suddenly he caught sight of her necklace and the jewellery she was wearing, and then the soldier asked her to give him all the jewellery. She recalled that she gave her finger ring and her earrings and her necklace and that is how the life of her son was spared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was the boy, did she say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, his age was 7 years of age at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the witness then said something to you about Sido's house; do you recall what she said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness said that after murdering three men, the soldiers turned to this line of women and children and they said that we should kill them now and they should stand properly in line, and when they were saying this, Sido said: "Don't do this to us; what have we done? I have gotten a house here and I will give you my house", and Witness B recalled that when she said this, her house was not burning at that time, but one of the soldiers ordered her house being burnt and her house was burnt with the help of something that was put on the rifle and fired and her house was burnt. Later on she corroborated the fact, witness D corroborated the fact, that Sida was also indeed killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this witness also had a concern question put to her that was not put to any of the other people present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say what that question was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was asked where her husband was and when she expressed her ignorance of the whereabouts of her husband, she was struck in her head by the soldier who had put that question to her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think again this witness confirmed that the soldiers discussed amongst themselves as to whether or not these people should be shot or, in fact, burnt alive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think again this witness confirms that the dead bodies of the four individuals were seen to be carried into a burning house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this witness also confirmed to you, did she not, that the remaining group of women and children were taken into the summer house which was duly locked by the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she also confirmed, did she not, Witness B's account of the breaking open of the door with an axe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she stated to you that the group spent two days in the forest nearby; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I think she stated, like indeed the other witnesses that we have heard about, that the group went to Pajtov Han where they were arrested by the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, indeed, this witness said to you that she was eventually rescued with the others by the United Nations Protection Force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she again confirms something about a discussion that took place between the HVO and the United Nations Protection Force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court what she said about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She recalled that the UNPROFOR soldier approached one of the HVO soldiers at the checkpoint at which they had been stopped, and asked him for letting these people go, these survivors of Stupni Do, and the soldier said that he could not do that without the prior permission of Ivica Rajic and Emil Harak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if we can now move on to witness E?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me ask a couple of questions regarding witness D. (To the witness): You mentioned a guard force of 30 to 40 people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the guard force? Were they part of the BiH or were they local persons who lived in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what the witness said. The witness said that they were all the native residents of Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not regular army of the BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She did not say that. She did not say that they were part of regular army of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that these soldiers who had HVO badges on them were dressed in camouflage. Was that green or black or neither? I think of camouflage as being, you know, a combination of, perhaps, green and brown, something that might go along with surrounding trees, but from reading the witness statements it seems that it may have been a different colour. You tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of the interviews with some of the other interviews, it appears that a distinction can be made between black uniform and camouflage uniform because there a number of witnesses who mention about soldiers being clad in black uniform. So this witness specifically mentioned it to be camouflage uniform, so my impression of it is it is the camouflage uniform which blends with the plantation and with colours around.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Cayley. You are proceeding to witness E?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness E. (To the witness): I think witness E is a young woman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, indeed, she was aged 14 at the time of the attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she was born in Stupni Do and had lived in Stupni Do all her life; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think witness E lived in a different area of the village to which we have been talking about already with the other witnesses. I wondered if you could indicate on the aerial photograph exactly where she did live, where witness A indeed said her place of residence in the village was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a portion of the village that was lower than the portion that we have been talking about and, according to witness E, the name of that portion is Zarnoger and her house here was 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bajwa. I think this witness noted something about the change in the uniform of the Police Officers. I think, your Honour, this may assist in the question you just addressed to the witness. Could you explain what the witness said to you about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that as a student of the elementary school what she remembered as Vares Majdam, she used to go to Vares Majdam daily to attend her school and her classes. She could not recall exactly when, but she said that she has only noticed that Police Officers who used to wear grey uniforms started wearing camouflage uniforms, and she also recalled that they had badges with Croatian chessboard and HVO written on them. She recalled that lots of these new policemen in camouflage uniforms were wearing crosses around their necks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this witness confirmed to you, did she not, that the night before the attack the electricity was cut off in the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think her mother commented to her at the time that if the electricity was cut off, then there was trouble ahead; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes she recalled that is what her mother said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the early morning of October 23rd the witness stated to you what she had heard. Can you explain to the court what she said to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in the early morning of October 23rd at about 8 o'clock, I think the witness stated what she heard. I wondered if you could say to the court what she said to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she recalled that morning at the start of the attack, she was piling wood logs just outside her house in the shed, and she heard some random shootings, and she thought that that shooting should be the one by those youths which used to do that in the village. But suddenly after those random shots, she said that suddenly lots of intense firing started and she recalled that firing was coming from Vares Majdam, from Bjelo Borje and from Mir and from all the different directions, and seeing so much of firing she rushed inside her house to see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the witness then stated to you, did she not, that her, her father, her sister and her aunt rushed to the basement shelter of the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think then the witness explained to you what happened next. Can you tell the court what she said to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that in the basement with her were her sister and the sister of her father and her father himself, and presently her father left saying that he is going to reinforce the defences of the village. With the departure of her father, the three women were left behind in the basement. She recalled that meanwhile all the windows had broken and all of them, all three of them, were lying on the wooden floor of the basement. Then she remembered that some of her neighbours arrived and she recalled the name of Nevzeta who came with her seven year old daughter. Then she recalled the name of Lejla who came with her one-year old granddaughter, Indira. Then she recalled the name of Merima who came with her son, Vahidin, and with her daughter, Mebrula. And all of them came, and with their arrival they became 10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this point she found out that there were soldiers very nearby where they were sheltering. How did she know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then she recalled that there was another neighbour who came and she said that she was in a very bad condition and her clothes were all ridden with dust and she was trembling. She said that, "They have entered, the HVO have entered the village". The witness, he recalled that that neighbour who came, she said that those soldiers were clad in black uniforms and they had white cloth ribbons tied around their upper arms and they had black caps on their heads. That is the description that was given to witness E at that time in point by one of her neighbours who arrived in her house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this point, indeed, the witness's neighbour noticed some soldiers around the house from which they had just fled; is that correct?
