utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it was decided at that point that they would, in fact, all leave the basement shelter because that neighbouring house was very close by to them and they thought they would, in fact, have an arrival of soldiers soon to them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the witness explained to you that she ran out of the basement and behind a rain barrel that was next to the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the court what she said to you happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She said that the moment that they saw soldiers in the nearby house everybody wanted to flee the basement where all of them were, and she also went out trying to flee the place. She saw a water barrel just lying beside the wall of the house in whose basement she was hiding, and she just huddled herself in one of the corner behind that barrel. She said that she could still be seen, she was not fully hidden, and she said that firing was still going on ad presently she felt as if a bullet had struck the barrel behind which she was hiding. Fearing that it had been hit, she recalled that she gradually crawled out of the barrel and she recalled that she did not know what to do. She was just squatting on the ground, and squatting on the ground she noticed that on her left side her dimija that she was wearing had been torn, and she could see that the skin where the dimija was torn was pierced and there was blood, a trickle of blood, there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think then a voice, in fact, called to her from the basement calling her back inside; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She said that it was her sister Medina and her aunt Hatioza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, in fact, the group of people in the basement then hid in a pit in the ground; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that the witness then explained that she heard masculine voices calling down into the basement. I wondered if you could explain something of that to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that at that time totally there were four, including witness E herself, and amongst which was her sister, her aunt and one of the neighbours, and all of them were crammed into that vegetable storage pit in the basement. She recalled that she was curled up and she was lying on the floor of the pit and on her was sitting her own sister who was covering her. She recalled that she heard these sounds of somebody saying: "Is there anybody in?" Then she recalled that it appeared as if the same person who had asked this question stepped into the basement into whose pit they were sheltered, and then she recalled the same voice calling somebody by the name of Kakanjac. She recalled that somebody replied to that call for Kakanjac and asked: "What?" and this man said: "I have found three balija women".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. So after the soldier actually called out, what did the witness say happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She recalled that suddenly she realised that there were two men inside the basement where these four women were hidden, and she realised that probably she was not visible to them because this man had only mentioned three balija women and not four, because actually there were four. So presently she recalled that they were swearing at these three women that they were looking at. She said that she did not hear any kind of a response or any kind of a voice of those three women who were on her and who were there and who were visible to those men. Then presently she recalled that she heard a burst of gunfire and later on it was all quiet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, indeed, the witness said to you that she called out to the three women that were with her in a low whisper and that there was no reply; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she then called to her sister again and there was still no response; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the witness then said to you that she had climbed out of the pit and she saw something unusual. Can you explain to the court what it was that she saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She recalled that she saw a candle with a flame flickering just beside the pit in which these three dead women lay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this stage the witness explained to you that she ran up towards Pricado which is, indeed, the previous image which was on the television screen in front of the court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen as she was running away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She recalled that she was wounded with -- her buttock had been pierced with a bullet so she slowed down while she was trying to run and escape. She slowed down and while she was trudging along the way up Pricado, she heard a voice, one man calling to another: "Go after her, catch her, kill her", and she recalled that suddenly after this there were bullets that were striking around the place where she was, and she again broke into a fast run and reached to the nearby forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she then moved to an area of the forest, in fact, a clearing in the trees above Stupni Do called Ravnica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there she met five to six soldiers. Could you explain to the court what she said to you about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she recalled that when she noticed those soldiers in that clearing of Ravnica just above Pricado, they were already jumping over the fence around that clearing. She had an impression that they had seen her. So she was about to run when those soldiers addressed her saying that, "surrender yourself". She said that, "When they said this, I was sure that they had seen me so I again starting running and they started shooting at me from behind".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this stage the witness met up with other villagers; she ran from this point and she met a lot of villagers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she decided to do something somewhat unusual and I wondered if you could explain what she decided to do next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She recalled that she was hiding inside the trees with a clump of trees, and suddenly it occurred to her that she should climb up the tree and see the village, what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, indeed, she had a panoramic view of the whole village from this beech tree; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court what she saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she recalled that she saw lots of fires in the village. She recalled that from her position at the top of the tree she could saw all the different portions of the village. She could see Pricado and Mlincic and Lipa in the main village itself, and she saw fires everywhere. She recalled the names of specific houses where those fires were, and suddenly she saw the roof top of one of the houses in the main body of the village which was called Guvno suddenly exploding and turning into pieces. That is what she saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think some time later she actually returned into the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where I think she met up with her father; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did she tell you about the house that she had fled from? I think she mentioned something to you about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she said that when she fled from that house at that time she only knew that there were three people who had been killed there, and that was because she was hidden with them. But later on her father asked her about the sister, about father's sister and about witness E's sister, and she said: "Both of them are killed". The father asked about some of the other neighbours who were hidden with witness E. She said she did not know at that time. But the same night, when they fled out of the village, the father went back to the house to see the dead body of her daughter, witness E's sister, and coming back, father of witness E told witness E that everybody else, nine people, were killed and their dead bodies were there in the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she then subsequently went to the basement of another house in the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a fairly large group of people sheltering in that basement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she then joined that group and eventually she explained that she reached Dabravine with the help of the United Nations Protection Forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. If we could now move on, please, your Honours, to witness F? Witness F, I think, is it correct that she was at the time of the attack a 41 year old woman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, indeed, she was a housewife. She describes herself as a housewife to you with two children in their early 20s; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she also told you, did she not, that both her son and her husband were killed in the attack on Stupni Do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she actually said something to you about the ethnic mix of the village prior to the attack on Stupni Do, in fact, I correct myself there, prior to the breakdown of the former Yugoslavia. I wondered if you could say something about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, witness recalled that there were about eight houses, Serb houses, in the village apart from one Croat woman married to a Muslim man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this witness also, and this was from her personal experience because both her husband and her son were in the village guard force, actually says something to you, she gives a description of the village guard force. Could you explain to the court what she says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, actually when the witness was asked concerning this aspect she said that there were soldiers in the village, but then she suddenly said that, "We should not call them soldiers, they were guards because all of them were from our village, none of them from outside the village, and they were just protecting their own village". She said that some of them did not have uniforms, and she recalled that her own husband and her own son, both of whom were members of that village guard, did not have uniforms. Both of them just had camouflage jackets without trousers. Then she recalled that her husband had bought somewhere boots for her son, but her son's foot size was bigger and the boots were shorter, so it was that kind of force that they had in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think on the night of 22nd October 1993, she indeed said to you that she was at home with her son, Muamer, and her husband Saley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she said to you, did she not, that in the morning she had to rise quite early because her son Muamer had to go for guard duty and she, in fact, had to cook his breakfast; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what she said to you about the departure of her son from the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were moments of deep distress for her to recall everything and she said that the son left the doors of the house saying, "Allah-I-Manad", and then she said: "I kept standing in the door looking at the back of my son", and the son went down and reached the road just beside the house and then he turned back realising that his mother might still be there. He, a second time, he said, "Allah-I-Manad", and then he went away. Then she started crying and saying that, "I never saw another time living or dead".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Her son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does "Allah-I-Manad" mean, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness was not asked this question, but otherwise it is a Bosnian variation of Arabic farewell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is a form of valediction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should mean "To the protection of God".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, thank you. I think the witness then said to you that her husband went to the area of village called Guvno and he took the keys to their stable with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she explained to you that she followed him to get the keys to the stable and then returned back to their house to prepare the coffee for the breakfast; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think her husband then returned and they sat down and drank their coffee for their breakfast. I think she said something very specific about the timing of the attack. I wondered if you could explain that to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she recalled that they had a clock with a cuckoo in their house, and she recalled that when they started sipping at their cups of coffee the cuckoo started cooing, and she remembered that distinctly, that it was 8.00 in the morning and a while later, while they were talking to one another, a shell fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, shooting started all around; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the witness then explained to you that her husband told her to go to Rasida's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, I think, indeed, this witness did go to the basement of Rasida's house and that basement, am I correct, was in fact decided into two rooms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there was one larger room and one smaller room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I think, in fact, other people arrived in this basement shelter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She talked about two women call Kada and Melca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think she then heard shooting all around again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the witness heard shouting. There were specific words which she remembered very clearly and I wondered if you could repeat those to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. She recalled that while in the basement she was just pacing up and down fearing for the lives of her husband and her son, and every now and then he would just dash towards the door to see what is happening outside. On one of these occasions when she was just standing by the door she heard lots of shoutings and yellings outside, and she recalled distinctly that it was "Uraa, Spremni Za Don", and the witness specifically said that this is the war cry of, what she said, "Ustashas".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I think this witness also confirmed that she heard screaming from Kava Likic's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, that is where nine people were killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this witness seeing that, as she called them, the Ustasha were close around the house, it was decided that all of the women and children would move into the back room leaving an older gentleman, Ramiz Likic, in the front room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this stage she heard the sound of boots upstairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think Ramiz Likic came from the front room to the back room and, indeed, told them to surrender and that the HVO had arrived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this stage the soldiers who came into the basement made both Ramiz Likic and all the women and children that were present come out of the basement to the outside of the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the soldiers say to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers asked them for money and for all their valuables and told them to surrender their jewellery, and they said that only those will live who will be able to produce at least 100 German marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this stage this older gentleman Ramiz Likic was taken to one side by the soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that they were made to stand in a line and Ramiz Likic was also, and Ramiz Likic happened to be the brother-in-law of the witness, was also standing in the same line and suddenly she heard a voice saying: "Step aside, you old man". Then she saw that the brother-in-law stepped aside, and then she recalled that he was asked for money and he said that he is an old man and he is just a pensioner and he does not have no money on him. Then she heard the sound of a shot being fired and she said that she was too scared to turn her neck and see what had happened to Ramiz. So she heard a voice saying that, "Still not dead" and a second shot, and then she said that she just glanced sideways and she saw Ramiz Likic lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this stage one of the soldiers who is in the group that was at this location says something that makes her realise that her son is dead. I wondered if you could tell the account that she gave to you about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness recalled that while they were collecting money and jewellery from them, one of the soldiers was saying that, "We have killed all of them and we have killed your bravest soldier". Then when he was talking about the bravest soldier, he said "Godiste 73". She said: "According to our language, Godiste 73 would mean the bravest soldier is the one who was born in 73". And then she said that he became more specific in saying Godiste 73, he said, "Mugdim". She said "I knew that there was nobody in the defence of the village or, indeed, even amongst the residents of the village whose name could be Mugdim". She recalled that since the name of her own son was Muamer, she just came to realise that it is her son, the bravest soldier, and who had also been born in 73, who was being referred to by the same soldier. That is how she came to know that he was dead and he had been murdered, he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this stage soldiers tell one of the women that she has to go to where the village guard was located and tell them to surrender; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, indeed, that particular lady could not go because she said she had two young children to look after; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, I think, indeed the witness was then chosen for this job; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, indeed, the witness told you that she started to proceed to where she thought the village guard force was located and she became very frightened because she saw a lot of soldiers around her; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give a brief description of what she said about the uniforms of the soldiers that she saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she said that they were wearing black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, indeed, she said that she was so frightened that she turned around to go back to where she had come from; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think at this stage a soldier said something to her and advised her not to be frightened. Could you explain what exactly happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The witness recalled that, frightened by seeing so many soldiers gathered at a neighbouring house, she suddenly turned back and as she turned back she saw this soldier, and she told that soldier: "I cannot go to communicate your message to our soldiers because there are other soldiers there and they might shoot at me". That soldier said: "Don't worry. They will not shoot at you. I am their commander." The witness was emphatic that the word that that soldier used was "Zapovgednik". She said that "Zapovgednik" is the name for the commander used by Croats. Then the witness recalled that she had been in a very strange state. She could not recollect things. She could not recollect features, but certainly when the soldier said, "I am the commander", she said: "I was suddenly shaken and I looked at this soldier who was describing himself as the commander of all this destruction". She said: "I was able to see the face of this soldier". She gave a description and the description that the witness F gave was that it was a middle-aged man; he had a broad thick set frame; he had hair that was dark brown in colour and he had a round face and at that time she said that he was wearing a beard that did not look dusty, it looked to be freshly trimmed. It was about two and a half centimetres. She said that he was wearing a uniform and some of the upper buttons of his shirt were open, and she recalled that by virtue of the fact that she saw this big cross shining on his chest, and she recalled that he spoke in a very low and in a very calm fashion and he was very soothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I think she, indeed, then does go to the village guard and, in fact, subsequently makes good her escape from the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do not intend to examine Mr. Bajwa as to the final statement in the bundle that we originally said we were, in fact, going to ask him to talk about, but I certainly think it is a statement that you will find of extremely useful guidance in respect of the village guard force, because the individual who gave the statement was a member of the village guard force. But he does not actually give any evidence of the atrocities in Stupni Do, specific evidence on atrocities, so I think in many ways it would be perfectly satisfactory for you to read it in your deliberations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: That is regarding witness G?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is regarding witness G, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Have you concluded with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have concluded with this witness, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then you may be excused, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Have you got a final complete question to him that he has recorded the statements of pseudonym witnesses A to G and that they were taken properly, that materially he did not add anything or subtract anything from their statements and they were recorded in the normal course, and that these witnesses originally, whoever they are, signed those? Has the composite question been put to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That question has been put to him, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Covering all of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, covering all of those aspects, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are excused. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, who will be your next witness? How long do you anticipate to hear from him or her?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The next witness will be examined by my learned friend Mr. Ostberg. I would estimate it would take approximately 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, why do you not call your next witness and we will hear from him, perhaps, for 15 to 20 minutes and then we will recess for lunch?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam President. If you could call Brigadier Ulf Henricsson, please? BRIGADIER GENERAL ULF HENRICSSON, called.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, General Henricsson. You may be seated. Mr. Ostberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Yes, I am ready to proceed. Examined by MR. OSTBERG

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are Brigadier General Ulf Henricsson?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I can see from your uniform, serving with the Swedish Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very good. Would you give the court a brief account of your military career?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am an army officer. I had made a normal career and became Colonel, head of the Armoured Combat School in '90. I got Brigade Commander for the 10th Mechanised Brigade in '91 and I got the assignment to organise and train the first Nordic battalion for Bosnia in April '93. I came down to Bosnia with a recognisance team at the beginning of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we now turn to your engagement with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you first asked, after you have done this training of the battalion, when were you put on the UN assignment for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my first assignment was when I got the job in April '93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To do the training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To do the training. That was a UN assignment. Then I started down here as a part of UNPROFOR in September '93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a commander of the Nordic battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you then based in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had our headquarters outside Tuzla and my area of responsibility was the same as the 2nd Bosnian Army corps, and it started north in the Posavina corridor in Brcko and down south, to some 10 kilometres south of Vares in central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have some maps we are now formally going to offer into evidence. We firstly start introducing a map of Bosnia and that is Exhibit 2. This is nothing but a map of Bosnia but on our screens you can just point where in Bosnia your battalion was based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is a very bad map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I will find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will have a more detailed one as exhibit No. 3, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Bad because you say it is small, it is difficult?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is bad too, but my area of responsibility started up here at Brcko, some 10 kilometres south of Brcko, and south to Vares down here, there, and then from the east, from Kalesija and over to about up to some 10 kilometres east of the border and then it followed the line of confrontation over this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used the term "line of confrontation". Give us a very short overview of the military situation in the vicinity of where you were deployed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The line of confrontation run in some, I think it was, 20 kilometres east of Tuzla and then north ------

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we now introduce a new map. You have already a new map, a better one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will give you another one to make it easier to go into details.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 2, are you going to offer that into evidence, that was the first map?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is a map that you have produced, I gather?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We have produced it, yes, your Honour. That was the one we firstly saw.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was that produced by the Prosecutor's Office, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 2 will be admitted. This is Exhibit 3 now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Another. Let us see if Brigadier General Henricsson says this is any better, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, it is. You recognised the first one. It is Bosnia!

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map over the town of Vares in the south of my area of responsibility, and my area of responsibility went in this area up to the village of Dastansko, and then it went down some 10 kilometres. If you put the map a little more on the south, my area of responsibility, you have the village of Stupni Do which was inside my area of responsibility, and we have the borderline to the British battalion in a village called Pajtou Han which is some 10 kilometres south of Vares, along the road running down to Breeza and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can see the road on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on the screen, but on this one, so if you move the map a little more down south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you do that? Can we do that? We cannot do that. But you can maybe as you describe it, do you have a -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you see the town of Vares, you have a road, and if you follow that road 10 kilometres south you have the limit, and the border of my area of responsibility in a small village called Pajtou Hahn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this area the confrontation line, and on the map, on the screen, it went about one kilometre east of Dastansko and run from north to south, and then it turned to in the village of, I have a name Bonikva, and one kilometre south of that road it went off to the east, and that is the line of confrontation in this area shown on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you want to go further west, we are told that you could put the map on the overhead projector. I gather this shows enough to show the confrontation line east. Do you want -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is enough to talk about what happened in Vares, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you want to go further west, you may, but you will have to use the overhead projector?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: But you do not have to; maybe we can adjust the one we have when we go into the details of Stupni Do. I just want to know the confrontation lines between -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was for us the confrontation line was between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian government, the Muslim, mainly, but in this area it was a Croat brigade, as a Croat enclave, and this brigade, the Bobovac Brigade, was under the command official by the 2nd corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us using the little map you have on the screen of the outlines of the authority of the HVO, the second command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the headquarter of the HVO was, then you have to put the picture a little more south if it is possible, it is just up north with the name Orsoya.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Really, I think it would be help us if -----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Is this enough for your Honours to see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but in the buildings north of the name, if you put it more north up there, yes, you were right. There you have it. There we have the headquarter of the Bobovac Brigade and of my own company command of the H company from Nordic at the same spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they based in the vicinity of each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was about 200 metres between our camp and the headquarters of the Bobovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell the court now the outlines of the authority of the Bobovac Brigade, of the entire HVO in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I cannot do it on this screen but I can take it on the big map here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, may be that would be of interest?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think for me it is of interest because, well, first I would want the witness to describe what is, as he calls it, a confrontation line. It would be helpful if he could draw or at least we could get the perimeters primarily because of your argument about the nature of the conflict, was it truly international, so it is important for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you, please, put this under the other -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the same scale as before.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Maybe we will stand in recess now. I think what would be helpful, at least for me, would be a drawing in some kind of a pencil, pen or something of the north, the east, the south and the west borders of the confrontation line during this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: And the HVOs, where they were and the authority of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. If we can get -----

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: In the recess we will ask the General to do that on the map which we will then tender as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is the simplest way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg, we were hearing from Brigadier General Henricsson. Are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I am ready to proceed, yes, thank you, your Honour. BRIGADIER ULF HENRICSSON, recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Brigadier General, you understand that you are still under oath, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then we are ready to resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. May it please your Honours, now we have put on the board a map with the lines put there by the Brigadier General. First, I will ask you, look at your screen in front of you ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and then point on the map on the board to say what part of it is on the screen -- on the one you have made the lines on, on that one, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Here we have the town of Varis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Have you before you on the screen also part of the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just outline on the big map what part of it is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is this part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. Then we know exactly where you are when you look on your own screens. Then go on, please, to tell me what do these lines, the red one and the green one and the signs mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The red line is a confrontation line between the Bosnian Serbs and the government controlled area with a mainly Muslim, but in this area, this area up here, was controlled by Muslim unit. This area was controlled by Croat unit, a Croat unit named the Bobovac Brigade, and then it was Muslim unit down here. The Croat unit was under the command of the 2nd Bosnian Army corps which had their headquarters up in Tuzla, here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Outside the other map, Tuzla is outside the other map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK, yes, very long, because we have that little map on the screen now, from here, but they were commanded formally from Tuzla but, in reality, somewhere else. This Muslim army corps, the third one, was commanded from Zenica. So we have a border between two government controlled army corps in this line.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So that we will have the record straight, to the left, that is green, is it, or blue? I am not colour blind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: It is green, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, to the left then, to the left, your left, my left of the green, then that is the area controlled, you said, by the Bosnian Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not correct ---

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- because this is the government controlled, the Bosnian government controlled, area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The whole map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the north and west of this red line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is north and west?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This part, this part of the map ---

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- is government controlled. This was controlled by the Serbs, but inside the government controlled area, there was a Croat enclave and a Croat HVO unit inside the Muslim areas which were (indecipherable) and up north from here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. So to the left then of the green is controlled by -- to the left of the green ---

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Croat controlled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: All of the left, to the left of the green?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And north of this line here, that is controlled by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then where the pink or red line is, to the right of that then would be controlled by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then there is an area right to the south of the green line and to the west of the red line, that would be controlled by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslims, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then to the north in between the green and the pink line would be controlled by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Are we in the clear?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think so. MR. OSTBERG (To the witness): Then I will ask you, my next question is, where was it, if any, fighting between Croats, I mean, Bosnian Croats, and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time the fighting ------

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking now about October 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and the fightings between the Muslim and the Croats was in central Bosnia in this area, from Viseko and down to Mostar -------

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you continue, maybe we should take, if I can have the help of the usher, down the map with the lines and tender that as Exhibit No. 3?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Those lines are the confrontation lines you have referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. The confrontation lines that the General is telling us about.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. You can take it down and we offer it as evidence - you can take it away and give it to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that going to be Exhibit 3 as modified?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No. 3, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As modified with the colours?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. (To the witness): Now on the board, then please, General, if you will continue, tell us what we have on the board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here we have a long confrontation line between the Bosnian Serbs on this side, the west side and then the government controlled Bosnia, and at this time it was heavy fighting between the Muslims and the Croats inside the government controlled Bosnia, in this area, Gorni Vakof, Vitez, in this area, and down to Mostar in this area. When we arrived here, it was a big tension between the Croats up in Vares and the Croats south of Vares. Even though they were thought to be under the control of the Muslims up from Tuzla, but it were tension, but the fighting had not spread up to Vares in the beginning of October '93.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What number is that, Mr. Ostberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We are not going to tender that as an exhibit. We just have it as assistance to the witness statement, because we have no copies of it and I cannot use it to give it as evidence to you. (To the witness): I think you have satisfied us now on the military situation. Can you now tell us on your of your own observations about what was going on in the area of Vares in the end of October 1993, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, we knew there were tension and in my first unit which arrived into this area were deployed down in Vares, north of Vares, on a camp which we took over from Canadians. The first position we took up was on the border between the Croats and Muslims, west of Vares and after, I think it was around 18th August, fightings broke out in this area two hours after the position were deployed, and the Muslims launched an attack on a small village called Kopijari. That was our first experience down here. So we knew that there were big tension in this area. During this time we were under deployment and we built up our knowledge about this area, and on 23rd October I was in Kiseljak at the Bosnia-Herzegovina command of the UN, and after lunch I had planned to go back to Tuzla and I then had to go through Vares because that was only possible road up. Then we got the message that it was not possible because the fighting had spread, so the road was blocked, but after some hesitation I got the message from one of my assistants that we could try to get out. We went off and come up to a village named Dabravine, some 30 kilometres south of Vares, where we were stopped again. We had the permission to go further and after 10 kilometres more we stopped again, this time by a Muslim patrol which said it was not possible to continue because of heavy fighting and on the road there we found a dead farmer and his cow. So I stopped and thought it was very unhealthy to go further with the soft skin cars. We turned back down to Dabravine where I met the commander, the Muslim commander, of the operational group south of Vares and he told me that there had been an attack on the village of Stupni Do from the Croats, and they just have started and planned a big attack at the town of Vares as a revenge. We talked about it a little and I got him with me on a plan that I could go up to Vares to see what had happened, see if there were any massacre or assault on the village of Stupni Do and then came back to report. So, I mounted a decision and we went on and it started to get dark, and when we came just south of Vares we saw the sky lighted by the burning village of Stupni Do. There was nothing to do there, so we continued up north to my company commander and company camp. I met my company commander, Major Birger, who just were on his way to the Croat Brigade, the Bobovac Brigade grade, which had their headquarter just some 200, 300 metres away from our own camp. He told me that now there were a new brigade commander in the Bobovac Brigade, a man named Ivica Rajic, and we came into the headquarters and started to negotiate with Ivica Rajic and he said that he was a commander of the operational group in Kiseljak and he now had taken command of the Bobovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall exactly how he introduced himself, the words he used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not exactly, but he was very clear that he was the new commander of the Bobovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He spoke what language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He spoke Serbia Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had an interpreter and that was Sergeant Ekenheim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We start to talk about what happened and I demanded to come into Stupni Do as soon as possible and he said it was not possible. He refused. I then told him the threat from the Muslims, that if I did not come into the town there would be a heavy attack on Vares, but he still refused. But after some time he agreed on letting us in the next day. So with that message, I went back to Dabravine, told the commander of UG in Dabravine what Ivica Rajic had said, and he was not satisfied with that. He demanded that I should go in this night. So I went back up to Rajic, told him: "I want to come in this night", but he still refused, and I then left with where I did not promise not to go in, and then he was very upset because he was not sure what we should do, and I got a very clear picture that he knew exactly what then happened up in Stupni Do because there were still fire, small armed fire and exclusion at that time in the night. He was very anxious to stop us from coming into Stupni Do. I went back to Dabravine once more that night and then negotiated a cease fire until the next day to come into Stupni Do. The next morning -----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just jump in and ask you, did you pass any area where you could have a look into Stupni Do so that could you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, no, because it had been dark and there was a lot of mines which hindered us to go up or manoeuvre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any flames or things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we saw the burning village, we saw the light from the burning village in the night. So in the morning we started an operation with two units going into Stupni Do from two different directions. They were stopped rather early but after some struggle they came just in the vicinity of Stupni Do, but were stopped by two Croat checkpoints with a mine, mines over the road. I and my company commander tried at the same time to manoeuvre to a position where we could look into the valley and the village. I managed to reach a position and before we went out we should have had a meeting with Ivica Rajic, but he was then not on his headquarter, as I were told. But when we stood on the hillside in Vares, I think it was an engineering officer of the brigade, he came very angry and said: "We are not supposed to be here" because in that place we saw with the binocular just into the village which was still burning. There were still some small arms fire from the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see some people also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was too .....

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Too far away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. While he, the engineering officer, he then said that now Ivica Rajic was in his headquarter and he wanted to speak with us. We went back and then he said: "Well, I will let you in", and with that promise in the afternoon on 24th October I left Vares and after giving some my, intention to my company commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had just met Rajic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you something to tell us about that, from that meeting, if he said something of what was going on or if he had some comments and things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, his comments not letting us into Stupni Do was that his preparedness for the defence of Vares was more important than letting us into Stupni Do. At the same time we also met soldiers or call them extremists, or what you say, because he had a gang with extremists from Kiseljak and Kakang with a map which was not regular soldiers in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean by "extremists"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not regular soldiers but more like gangsters with skin clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, black skin clothing and even from other stuff with knives, hand grenades and guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were armed and they were -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were very heavy armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No real uniform of the usual battle type?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you could not even find them as HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went back up to Tuzla, my company commander continued to act down in Vares. On the evening, on Sunday evening, when I got back to Tuzla, I got the message at, I think, 10 o'clock that my units down in the town had been shot at by the Bobovac Brigade, a real attack against the UN unit, and they drawback from the central town of Vares. They had even attacked an ambulance very clearly marked with a red cross. I gave a company commander permission to leave the town at that time, but to defend the tunnel between the town and my company so we would not be enclosed. I also gave him an order to talk with the brigade commander, Ivica Rajic, and tell him that from now we will always only have live firing, no warning shots any more, and he did it. There was a lot of shooting over the camp but not at the camp during this night. On the morning I gave the company commander an order to deploy in central Vares again. I went myself to on the Serb side to Zvornik where we had planned negotiation with the Serbs. When I came back late in the afternoon to my headquarter, I got the message from my staff that my units in Vares has been forced to leave central town again after a very heavy threat from the Croats, and at that time we had another problem, and that was about 250 Muslim men jailed up in the town into schools in central town. We had deployed patrols outside these schools but they had been forced away. Then I ordered the company to redeploy in Tuzla but on safer -- in Vares but on safer spots outside and higher up so that they could look in the town and still have control without any risk, and went off from Tuzla to Vares. On the night, on 25th, I met Ivica Rajic again with my company commander -- sorry, I did not met Ivica Rajic then, I met Bozic, his second in command. He said: "I am now appointed Brigade Commander". I asked: "Where is Ivica Rajic?" He did not tell me. He was back in Kiseljak or something like that, he told me. He said everything is solved. The UNMO, UN concern, had been let into Stupni Do, and I did not know about that, but my company commander told me that that was only partly true. They had been let in by Ivica Rajic, but just to the first two houses where they found, as I learned, two dead bodies and then Ivica Rajic had stopped the visit in Stupni Do. So I still demanded to came into Stupni Do and Bozic promised us to come in, and we pointed a meeting at 9 o'clock in the morning and then we should go into Stupni Do at 2 o'clock p.m. and at the same time we should be let in to see the situation of the prisoner in the town. At that time we did not trust them at all, so we had already planned for an action to take us into Stupni Do, whether the Croat allowed us or not. So, 9 o'clock, I went to the Bobovac Brigade again. At the same time I ordered two platoons to go towards Vares on two different routes, one from the north and one from the west. When I came to the Bobovac Brigade, as usual the brigade commander was not there, he was not prepared to meet me, but I stuck to it and demanded to see him. After some minutes he was there and they said: "Well, you are allowed to come in but without gun and without machine gun of my interpreter", and I denied, "If you do not want me, will let me in with guns then we can negotiate here out". After some time they let us in with weapons and then Bozic again said we will be let in but not until 2 o'clock. So we waited, but some minutes before 2 o'clock where we were at the Bobovac Brigade, they backed again and said: "Well, we have to wait for the ECMM monitors to come in", but then I refused because I am still convinced that they already had stopped them in some checkpoint that they should not arrive, and with my threat then they stopped it and we went away to Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last conversation you had when you were informed that the ECMM were coming, who was that with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was with Bozic. At this time Ivica Rajic was not able, but both on Monday night and now we had a very strong feeling he was in the house, and after the meeting on Monday evening where Bozic had been rather co-operative, after some hours we got a threat letter from the same brigade that if we did not stop this we should be wiped out from earth so that was always, first, they agreed and then they stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came up to the last checkpoints near Stupni Do, and I went with my platoon which came in from the north. My military assistant, Major Eckenheim, he had a patrol from NORDBAT and from the UNMOs, from ECMM, which went to the schools, even I think with people from Red Cross. When we arrived to the last checkpoint we were stopped again, and they told us that, first, they would not let us in at all, then I said: "I will go in". They said: "Yes, but only with one vehicle" but they still refused to remove the mines and then I said: "If you do not remove the mine, I will shoot them away", and then they moved them off. I had ordered my platoon commander which was behind me to come in half a metre behind very close together, all vehicles, so we then got in very rapid with all four vehicles into Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That happened about 3 o'clock p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 25th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 26th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 26th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 25th, that was Monday. Then we still were refused to come in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was on 26th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the attack was on 20 -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 23rd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you tell the court about what you saw in Stupni Do when you went in there?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Brigadier General, if I may ask you a few questions before you get to that point to see if I understand your testimony: on October 23rd you were in Kiseljak-- pronounce it for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Kiseljak was controlled by the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but UN headquarter of Bosnia was situated in Kiseljak and that is where I were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was controlled by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The town of Kiseljak was controlled by the Croats, but the UN headquarter was under UN control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. You learned first about the attack on Stupni Do from a BiH commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He told you that the Bosnian Croats had attacked Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would have been on 23rd or 24th when you learned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 23rd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 23rd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of the Bobovac Brigade before Rajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not have his name. I had met him, but in the testimony from my company commander I think his name is in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the name are known by the Tribunal in the testimony from my company commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is not really important. What is important, though, is that at one point you were told that Rajic had taken over and was then the commander, is that not so, of the Bobovac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned that from my company commander on 23rd when I came up to Vares about 6 o'clock p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Bobovac Brigade is regular Bosnian Croat army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were based in Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that at one point you met Rajic and he had a gang of extremists with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you described these extremists as -- why do you not repeat that for me tell me what you mean by "extremists"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People with no conscience and dressed, well, if you see those motorcycle bands, about that, with skin clothing, but with machine guns, knives, hand grenades, pistols, with no common uniform, mainly black clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they wear white bands on their arms or somewhere, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember that just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were dressed in black?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Carrying knives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Knives? They did not look -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Knives, machine guns and everything they could take.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Rajic had them with him, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They arrived at the same time as Rajic, and we got that information both from our own observations, from our soldiers and even from the HVO soldiers which was not very happy with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but they must have come over Serbian territory from Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they? When you say "they arrived", they arrived where, at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the whole town of Vares, we had them. They moved around, but we saw them often at the headquarter of the Bobovac Brigade, the same men which we later met down in the town in checkpoints and so on, and they were very aggressive and some of them sometimes said: "Well, you are not allowed to come into Stupni Do because we have some cleaning to do before".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that commander Rajic was in charge of these extremists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he said it, very obvious and even -----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said he commanded the Bobovac Brigade. He had control over the area and his headquarter was guarded by those guys. We saw the same cars at this hotel which was their headquarter. I saw them inside this restaurant which served as headquarter, and they were in the restaurant part at the same time we negotiated in a part of this restaurant. So they are jostling together. They did what he said to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give me an example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because he commanded them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. He commanded them, you say, because they were there in the headquarters and he had said that he was commander of the Bobovac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were there occupying the same place as the Bobovac Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that he had a gang of these extremists whom you had seen in the Bobovac Brigade headquarters at a check point, is that correct, with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the checkpoint, not with Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was not there at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were the same ones ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that you had seen at the Bobovac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: General, I have no knowledge of military matters. When you talk of a brigade, how big a force would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question because all brigades down here is different, but if I said it is something like in between 500 to 2,500 men, and I think the Bobovac brigades consisted of about 800 men, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then when you used the expression "extremists", you did not mean by that people with any special political views? You described them in terms of their dress?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you can in this case only guess because we had no political discussion about it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So when you were at that checkpoint then, when you saw these extremists that you have described -- I am looking at your statement that is part of the material that was submitted to Judge Sidhwa -- you say "the extremists said they had 'some cleansing to do'"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall them saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you interpret that word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my interpreter, Sergeant Eckenheim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you heard the word "cleansing" what did that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It meant that they were, well, removing, whether they did burning, perhaps, bodies and taking bodies away the evidence in Stupni Do. That was what I thought was meant with their saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was on October 24th, the day after the attack on Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember not the exact day, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was after the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was after. I think it was on Monday, but I am not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later on October 26th speak with some refugees from Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not myself, but on 26th in the morning I had sent out a patrol to pick up refugees from Stupni Do south of Vares, because the commander in Dabravine has asked us to do it because it was Croat controlled area and he knew that there was about 30 refugees, he said, so I sent my MA with some APCs, I think six in the morning, and they found 25 refugees which they brought down to Dabravine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall saying in the statement that you submitted that was a part of the material presented to Judge Sidhwa that, "Two young women stated that Stupni Do was attacked by regular fighting but in the evening the 'butchers arrived' and there was burning, looting, raping and killing. The two women both about 20 years old said that they had been raped". Do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I got that information from Major Ekberg who was in charge of this operation. I got it in second-hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. You do not know who these "butchers" were, do you, who were identified as butchers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not the exact person, but I am very sure that it was extremists from Kiseljak and Kakang.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same extremists you described before ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- as having been at the Bobavac Brigade headquarters ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- is that correct, and then the ones you saw at the HVO check point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have nothing further at this time. You are moving into another area, Mr. Ostberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. (To the witness): What I would like you to tell the court is what you actually saw when you more or less forcibly entered Stupni Do with your platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw a totally destroyed village. I think it was around 54 houses in that village, all of them more or less destroyed. We rather soon run into dead people, burnt bodies. We found three killed women in a cellar and I spent about 30 minutes at that time in Stupni Do because I had to hurry up to Dabravine to report to the UG to stop any further attacks. So I then left Stupni Do after seeing enough. Then we sent in two platoons which guarded Stupni Do until the investigation team arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you walk through the whole village of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not the whole, but mainly, the main part of the village I saw directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You can see from the map that this is one road running through the village with houses on either side of the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you walked this main road through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many houses did you enter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I entered I think one, but we were very cautious here because it was a big risk for booby-traps; that is mines or something like that. So we waited for a mine clearing team to come in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said the houses were destroyed, by fire, by grenades, by shooting, with other weapons, in what way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were so destroyed that it was hard to see after that short examination, but mainly by fire and perhaps explosion brought in and attached by people inside. But it was not mainly done by shelling; it was by burning and perhaps explosives on the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, would you by that say that the houses were set on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any idea what kinds of methods they used to set them on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I can just guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I recall you saying somewhere that you said some special colour of smoke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Well, I cannot recall that, but it was very heavy smoke in the town, and I think then that the investigator was rather confused in some aspects because it must have been a very high heat in some houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see some people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, no, no people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cattle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some cattle, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Living and hurt and dead cattle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All kinds: hurt, dead and living cattle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many cows or sheep or whatever it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not count them, but it was something between zero and 10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you entered at least one house. Did you find something special?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any dead bodies in this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the house, no. What I saw was I think two burned bodies outside the houses, and then women in the cellar. That was what I personally saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But no people in the village; no refugees or somebody coming, walking, civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about refugees being -- if I recall correctly ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: --- you said something about refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the morning of 26th we picked up 25 refugees south of Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Outside Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside Stupni Do, and they had fled Stupni Do when the assault was launched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
