utterances.text: So they were coming down from the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the hills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: --- from the hills?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Outside Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not rescue any refugees inside Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned some other units. When you went in, were you the first on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what kind of a UN or other units did enter Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, behind me were one of my own platoons and when I left Stupni Do the other way out I ordered another platoon which were blocked on another mine, mine checkpoint, to go over the railway and join the other platoon. So at about 16 hours I had two platoons up in Stupni Do, and they stayed I think until 27th or 28th where we got reinforcement from a British Company under Major Hunter because my soldiers were then very worn out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Understandable. Will you, before I conclude my questioning, summarise your meetings with Ivica Rajic? How many were they in total?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were I think four in total: two on the evening of 23rd and two on Sunday 24th. On 25th it was Bozic who said, "I am the new Brigade Commander", but my company commander had more meetings with Ivica Rajic than I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that another shift of Commander of the Bobovac Brigade did take place, or did you believe what Bozic said, that he was now the new commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I am convinced that we had Ivica Rajic in the rooms on the other side of the wall saying to Bozic what he should do. That is my guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any hesitation in your mind of who was in charge of the HVO forces during and after the raid of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we first met the first time we discussed a little about what had happened, and the right to do it and so on, and he pointed on his jacket where he had a black mark and said, "Do you know what this is?" "No", I said. "Well, this is a sign of anybody who has lost a close relative" or what he said, "so I have the right for this." But it is ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the area with your battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean at all? I left ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this, after this event, after the end of October, did you stay on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left Bosnia at the end of, well, in the end of March, beginning of April in '94.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any idea what happened to Ivica Rajic, where he went, after the Stupni Do event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We heard rumours or I would say it was more information from BH Command in Kiseljak that he had been seen in Kiseljak and lived down there, and perhaps still was the Commander of the unit in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he had his military command even after this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I heard, but in that case I think BH Command can answer better than I.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, General. I have no further questions. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Brigadier General Henricssion, you are excused. Thank you for coming today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg, would you call your next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, we would be happy to proceed. Our next witness is Sergeant Ekenheim also a Swedish soldier. SERGEANT RUZDI EKENHEIM, Called.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. EXAMINED BY MR. OSTBERG.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your name is Ruzdi Ekenheim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell the court what you are doing, what occupation is for the moment? What do you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment I am a sales rep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A sales representative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. Will you give us a very short summary of your military experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served with the Swedish Army between 1988/89 as a conscript. Further on I signed up again in 1992 to go to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On a UN mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On a UN peacekeeping mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With NORDBAT?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That was with a Swedish headquarters company that was established from the beginning in Sarajevo and then moved to Belgrade, then moved to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was which year did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in September '92.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually from 1st September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Your service with the UN, as what were you hired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served as Assistant Interpreter, bodyguard and so on for first for Brigadier General Pellnas [sic] who was chief UNMO. I served with him for one year. Right after that I went to NORDBAT 2; same occupation, I worked for Brigadier Henricsson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Interpreter and assistant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And bodyguard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bodyguard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then with the rank as Sergeant as today or had you some other rank then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the same rank. I was made Second Lieutenant. I refused to become an officer and moved back to Sergeant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You said that you served as an interpreter. Will you tell the court something about your lingual abilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I speak Serbo-Croatian, Serbian-Croatian Bosnian, whatever. I understand Macedonian, Russian, German, English, Swedish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come you speak so many languages? Tell us of your origin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My origin?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on July 11th 1967 in New York City, New York State, United States of America.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My grandparents on my mother's side come from Sarajevo and Osijek in Croatia. My biological father is from Montenegro. My mother was born in Austria, raised in Argentina and lives in Sweden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are certainly a real cocktail!

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With your work with the UN it was important that you spoke Serbian-Croatian and English of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from Swedish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me about your services with General Henricsson whom we have just listened to in this court. When did you join him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started work for him on September 27th 1993. The first time I met him was on the frontline in Kiseljak; North Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What date was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: September 27th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 27th September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started working for him on 27th and I met him on 29th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stayed with Henricsson?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed with him and his predecessor, Colonel Svensson who became Battalion Commander after him, up until NORDBAT 2, up until July 15th '94.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then quit your service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I went back to Sweden and stayed there for eight weeks and got assigned a new mission, to observe a mission in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And went on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until March 1st '95.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. Then we know what you have been doing with the UN. Now we will take you to the environment of Vares in October 1993. Tell me exactly what were your duties there then in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that particular time around Stupni Do incident and Vares incident, we had been down to Kiseljak, BH Command, and we went up to visit the Canadian Battalion Headquarters. I was there accompanying the Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Travelling with him in the same ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Travelling with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: --- in the same vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do the driving also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us which day will you say this was going when you travelled like you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am pretty bad on dates, so I would say this is day one of the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. We have fixed 23rd October for the event of Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That it is the 23rd October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I will ask you to tell me when you first did any observation pertaining to the village of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first observation was when we were supposed to leave the Canadian camp in Viseko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Viseko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Viseko south of the Vares area, north of Viseko. We bumped into some observers, UNMOs, who told us that the road ahead was blocked. I received orders from the Brigadier to go up north through the road to see what was going on and see if the road real was blocked. I came up to a village called Simin Han, that is Simin Han, Pajtov Han, that is about 7 klicks south of Vares. When I got up there and I noticed there was a combat zone ahead of me, I contacted the nearest Bosnian Army Headquarters to find out what was going on, and if we could pass through the area. At first we were denied because the combat zone moved south of my own location eventually. I started arguing with them, but finally got ahead to go. Went back to Kiseljak, picked up the Brigadier and a convoy that was standing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you made this trip was that on your own or were you travelling with someone else in the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a Swedish observer with me at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but that was myself from the Unit. I went back, picked up the Brigadier, the convoy. We came up to this village again and was stopped because the fighting had intensified along the road. At first we were denied clearance to go through. We got the clearance, moved ahead about another 3 klicks. If you do not understand what I am saying "klicks"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We do not. Please explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Klicks" is kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we know. Klicks.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If I told you I do not know what a kilometre is, how do you translate that? I am learning though!

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A kilometre is about a thousand yards; maybe a bit less than that. About 14, 1500 yards. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It sounds good to me!

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I am not used to yards! Ten kilometres is 6.2 miles I am informed from my American friend here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Now we know. Use the term "kilometre" for my understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I know what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we were stopped again at another check point, the whole convoy, and we refused to go further on. Fighting was about 150, 200 metres ahead of us intensifying. There was a dead man by the road, a dead cow. Some mortar grenade had just exploded there about two minutes before our arrival. After a couple of minutes the Brigadier decided to turn back the convoy and switch men and vehicles. So we left them with our unarmed vehicle and took on a Sisu, that is a normal APC. We got the clearance again from the Bosnians and then we got the first brief, the first part of second briefing about what was going on in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who briefed whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnians briefed us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Us" was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me and the Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told us that the Croats had attacked the village of Stupni Do and that the fighting going on along the road was the Bosnian attempt to come to rescue the village. They begged us to start an investigation and try to do what we could to stop the ongoing events, which we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the ongoing events,? What did you observe of these ongoing events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I do not think you have to use the map. Tell us about what you saw of what was going on in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From that point we could not see Stupni Do because that was on the other side of the hill, but you could clearly see the smoke, the fire because it was becoming dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you hear some shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could hear shelling, the firing, more explosions, normal war zone sounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what you mean by the ongoing event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw smoke, you heard firing, you heard explosions and things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Naturally the Brigadier promised to do whatever he could to look into what was going on. So then we passed through the Bosnian checkpoints on the way up to Vares, and there was I would say total emptiness along the road. The houses along the side were burning and we could see the village of Stupni Do burning in the distance. It was quite dark at that time. We got up to our Company headquarters. First on the way up we passed a Croat checkpoint. We got up to Eighth Corps Headquarters Camp and got another briefing from them what was going on in the area which was almost the same thing as the Bosnian Croats. Instantly the Brigadier demanded a meeting with the Commander of the Bobovac Brigade who was Ivica Rajic. Later on during the evening we got the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You met him then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did the interpretation between these two gentlemen, Rajic and Brigadier Henricsson?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eventually ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the court -- what we have heard so far in this court today is what you interpreted. So tell us now again how did Rajic introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He introduced himself as Ivica Rajic, Commander of the Bobavac Brigade. He recently replaced the old Brigade Commander and he said he was from a Special Police Unit from Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the way he introduced himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go on?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He said he was in charge of Special Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was from a special police unit Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what that Special Police Unit was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, your Honour. They call everything "police", everything "Special Forces", "Special Police". The definition of "Special Forces", "Special Police" in Bosnia is very wide.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Brigadier asked to get the information from their point of view, what was going on in and around the Stupni Do area. We were told that he thought, he knew actually, that the Bosnian Army was going to launch a major attack over the village of Stupni Do, that they had assembled a large quantity of soldiers, equipment and so on south of the village. That was naturally false.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the Brigadier General react to this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said it was bullshit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Clear enough. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because there would not be such as that in the area. Since we had just arrived from south of Vares to Stupni Do we had been eyewitness to what was happening along the road. Ivica Rajic continued to say that we have the right information, this is some intelligence, Special Forces intelligence again and stuff like that. The Brigadier said: "This is not right. We have the proper information. There is no attack going on here and we demand that we have a ceasefire right away." First Rajic agreed upon that, to have a ceasefire, then he changed his mind again and said that there would be no ceasefire. After a couple of arguments he agreed to having a ceasefire later on the same night, but then demanded that we go to the Bosnians and get a ceasefire from their side and have them stop any major attack over Stupni Do. The Brigadier approved of this. We went back to the Bosnians and they did not have any major attack ongoing. They were just curious to know what was happening with the people, civilians in Stupni Do, since there were no military installations, no military at all; it was just a village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So they actually agreed right away to have the ceasefire. We went back, supposed to go back up to the Croats in the Bobovac Brigade to deliver the message. On the way up we got stopped at an HVO checkpoint. After a minute, a minute and a half, we smashed the checkpoint. We went further up a couple of klicks where we met, came up to another checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again "kilometres"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kilometres, sorry, where we came to another checkpoint. We got stopped again. This time they put mines in front of us. They said we had no authorisation to pass up to Vares through a checkpoint, and the only person who could give us that permission was Ivica Rajic. He was not present at the time. The Brigadier got pissed and said: "We have to get through here. Either you move the mines or we will do the results." They got the in touch with the headquarters and again said, "No, you can't pass." So me and the Brigadier jumped out of the APC and we moved the mines ourselves. Then we went back into the APC, went up to Bobovac Brigade Headquarters and met Ivica Rajic, told him that the Bosnians have agreed upon the ceasefire, they have no major, no attacks whatsoever that is ongoing or imminent. He did not believe it at first and then he said "OK, ceasefire". Then we started arguing about the time of the ceasefire. We want an immediate ceasefire; they want it the next day. Then we started discussing what the details of the ceasefire. They wanted us to set up soldiers from our own unit in the village of Stupni Do; the best case being in Stupni Do with their own vehicles. First, Ivica Rajic agreed upon that. Then he changed his mind and said "No". The next suggestion was that we should go up in our APCs to the beginning of the village on the northern side; park our vehicles there and put the civilians in there; have them walking out from other buildings from the same village, walk them up to our APCs and then take them inside. It was dark; it was in the middle of the night. We refused, the Brigadier refused, because that would have been a suicide mission. The impression we had that is what they were waiting for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the evening of the first day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The evening of the first night; the first day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then? Then we turn to the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are not done yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are not done yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are not done yet. Then we started arguing with him about that and he went berserk, upset, I should say, he did not want to continue the meeting. So we went back to the Bosnians to inform them what was going on and how far they had gotten. When we went back to the Bosnians they were kind of hysterical because they were receiving more information about what was going on in Stupni Do. The information we received that there was slaughtering of civilians. That was about 3 o'clock, 3.30 in the morning. There was not much else we could do at that time. At the same time we received information from the local commander that there was a group of refugees on a hill across the graveyard on the way up to Vares, and he asked us to do what we could to save them. The Brigadier immediately responded to this first in the morning, daylight. We came back to the camp at 4 o'clock in the morning. At 6 o'clock I was ordered to go back and do a search and rescue mission. We went out with four APCs to the approximate area where we understood the refugees were available at. We blocked the road in both vans, start screaming and shouting and making sounds to get the attention of the refugees. After a while, about an hour, nobody came down. Two Croatian soldiers came down from the other side, HVO. We took them under protective custody. At the same time the refugees were coming down from the mountain. They were falling down from the hill, falling down into the river. We picked them up from our side, put them in the APCs and went back to Simin Han, south of Vares in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 19. The youngest was about five, a girl, and the oldest was about 85 years old, a man. When that was done we came down to the village and dropped off the refugees. Me and Major Ekberg was in charge of the search and rescue unit went in to interrogate some of the refugees. We picked one girl to talk to her. She told us her story -- do you want me to go into that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just an outline. Did you interpret the interview that Ekberg, the Major, had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Summarise what you learnt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She got caught up by HVO soldiers, forced into a house, with the first rape in front of her family's eyes, her dad, her ma, her brother and boyfriend, and they told them, "One sound from you while this is ongoing we're going to shoot you." After that they raped her, they raped her and then this happened. Then they killed her family one by one, telling her "If you cry one tear we're going to shoot you. That was done to force her and a group of 13 people into a building, a house, sit there, house on flames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the people in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the people lying in it. They found an axe in the house and got out, started running to the hills, to the wood. The Croats were following them in the woods. There was a lot of people running around in the woods at that time. They could hear the Croats following them in the woods, finding people here and shooting them on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people did you interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two. What you now told us was the story of the girl?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were two girls actually. We started interviewing the second one but we could not interview her because she broke up.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In your statement did you say that they raped her mother as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So that was these two interviews you took part in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two out of 19 people that you rescued from the hills?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you might go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we went back up, supposed to go back up to Vares, and we came to first major checkpoint, got stopped, smashed it, continued up to Vares. When we went to Vares, Maradam, that is the southern part of Vares, we got blocked in a major checkpoint which was hastily set up by Croatian Military Police, Croatian Units that was taking part in the ongoing events. So we got stopped there. They started placing people, RPGs, machine guns anti-aircraft guns in front of us and we were not allowed to move either backwards or forwards. I jumped out of APCs and started talking, and negotiating with them, but it was a dead end. Then we radioed to headquarters and asked them to get Brigadier Henricsson to go to Bobovac Brigade and start negotiating with them, which he did. While we were waiting for the outcome of this meeting we were naturally getting ready for combat. After 40 minutes, 45 minutes, a guy comes up in a white Volkswagen Golf, starts screaming and shouting and threatening us, if we do not leave his city he is going to kill us. Then he wants to start beating me up with an RPG.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Beating you up with a what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: RPG?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a grenade launcher, anti-tank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is about 90 centimetres long. The calibre is 76 millimetres. He puts it on his shoulder, blasts it off and there goes the tank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To beat you with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was he hitting you with it or threatening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was attempting to do it, but the other HVO soldier at the point stopped him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: So were you never beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were threatened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At this time because two police officers at the scene, they were from Vares themselves, so I overheard one of them telling the other one: "If he doesn't stop within five seconds I am going to shoot him myself. I don't want to lose my life because of an idiot." So he was speaking of this HVO soldier. So he just jumps into his car and drives off. A couple of minutes later Brigadier Henricsson and I think it was Chief of Staff or something at Bobovac Brigade came to the scene. We went back to Bobovac brigade to talk to Ivica Rajic and negotiate with him about entering the village of Stupni Do. At first he was not there. We went back to the camp, came back, he showed up. So at this point I think he agreed upon to letting us into the village later on the same afternoon. This is day two. We were supposed to meet him in the morning under -- no, that is wrong. That is another day. They were supposed to take us in. He never showed up. We went to Bobovac Headquarters to see his whereabouts and we got the answer he was in the field, that is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not meet him at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not. OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went back into Vares trying to get on high ground so we could see into the village of Stupni Do, because there was so much smoke at the time coming from the village it was impossible to stand close and watch it. You could not see anything. During this attempt to come up from high ground we were kind of chased up by two HVO Croat soldiers who asked us to leave, "You're not supposed to seeing anything." Then we went back to the camp and got a new meeting with Ivica Rajic. Then he agreed to let us in the village later on again at the night and we said, "Thanks, but no thanks." We suggested another time while it was still daylight. He refused. On several occasions during these discussions there was some tense feeling, and Ivica Rajic clearly stated on several occasions, I have to say this in Serbian, if you do not mind? He says: "Ja sam chef ovu parade" which means, "I am in charge of this parade.” That is a Yugoslavian expression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For being in charge of something going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It means we could not tell him what to do as well. Right after that we came back to the camp. Now it was almost night time. There was nothing we could do. Then we decided to -- the meeting had agreed upon to let us into the village at 8 o'clock the next morning, the third morning, and we were supposed to have a rendezvous south of Vares, Vares Majdan is the name of the place under the railway bridge where Ivica Rajic himself would escort us up to the village. We showed up. No Rajic. We went back up to Bobovac Brigade Headquarters. He was still in the field. Nobody knew where he was at. They had no means of contacting him. We went back trying to get into the village from different sides which was impassable because they sealed off the village effectively. Later on we went back again to the Bobovac Brigade Headquarters, found Ivica Rajic and he then agreed upon to let us in immediately to the village but only one vehicle and it was supposed to be the Brigadier. We were to be escorted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in the same car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Then we were to be escorted by his own troops. When we came up to checkpoint, the last checkpoint before the village, the person at the checkpoint refused to clear the mines in front of us. They told the security officer who was the man who followed us up there, they did not take any orders from him; they only took orders from Ivica Rajic. I was present at the scene when that happened, when they said that. Right after that I started arguing with the security, chief of security since he was only supposed to let one vehicle, one APC, the Commander's APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An APC is a car to transport people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, an armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people can be in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you pack them real good 25.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 25 at the most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you pack them real good, but they are made for about 12 I think, excluding the crew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The crew is how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that was the first vehicle and only vehicle they were supposed to let in. So then started moving, we moved the mines, and then the second APC came up to so close to the Commander's APC that there was no chance for them to separate the vehicles. Then the whole platoon moved into the village.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you get to another line of questioning, Mr. Ostberg, we will stand in recess for 15 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We now enter Stupni Do, and would you please tell us about what you saw when you entered there? Tell us first of all, the whole platoon, did I get that clear, the whole platoon went in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our guess was about eight to 10 vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Eight to 10 vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 35, 40, 50 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Were you in the first vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the first vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With Brigadier Henricsson?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then tell us exactly what you yourself saw and what you did when you entered Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first thing I did was to start searching the first house on the left side to see if there was anybody in there, checking for booby traps and stuff like that which they normally set out, bury down and things like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give us an idea of what is a booby trap?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A booby trap is, let us say, hidden explosives which explode by movement, by sound which is devised to explode if somebody touches, let say, body part or something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To prevent people to touch things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They want to kill you with that thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you do you are killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is just like mines. Started searching the first house for survivors and booby traps. We did not find anything there. So then we just kind of started walking down the village, searching each house on the side. After a couple of metres, let us say 10 to 15 metres, we found the first place where they burned somebody. It was just a pile of ashes on the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A former human being?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As ashes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All burnt and you could identify it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were ashes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could see that it had been once a human being?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The next I would say another 10, 15 metres down the road there was another burnt man that was laying in a ruin of an ex-house. He was booby trapped by himself. He had hand grenade in his armpit. That one was pretty badly damaged because a lot of wild dogs had been eating him the previous days. Then we were kind of in the middle of the village and started searching house by house. We found three women in a basement killed. Another man was lying outside in I would say in the ruins of another house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that you got out of your car and did all these things, you are now telling us, on foot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Then I started kind of searching house by house together with the rest of the unit, and all in all we found about 15 dead people in the village. Right after this we had another unit waiting on the first rendezvous point, south of Stupni Do, on the railway bridge. So the Brigadier decided to go down with the APC to that point and bring them up. So he went away with the APC say on the northern road which leads down to the south ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Down to the south?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: South of Vares to meet up with the APC unit down there. I decided to walk the whole village and through, let us say, bits, pieces of the forest by myself to see if I could find something along the road, either bodies, corpses or booby traps, mines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you now out of the main street of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it on or outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside the main street of Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. On the back side of a line of houses or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no houses in between Stupni Do and Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point I came down to the rendezvous point, about the same time as the Brigadier did, and there were two HVO soldiers guarding the road. They placed mines in front of the same railway track. The Commander told them to remove the mines so we could pass up to the village. They refused. Said: "We can only take orders from Ivica Rajic." The Commander said that they should be stupid because we were already in the village. They could see our vehicles in the village. We came from the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went out in the other direction and then you had people going in from the other direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came from northern side, passed through the village, down through the southern side where we met up down in Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They would not let you in from the southern side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the last orders they had received from Ivica Rajic was to not let us in to Stupni Do. We just told them that this was just stupid because we were already in the village. If they turned around they would see our vehicles in the village, and we obviously came from the village. They still refused. The Brigadier got kind of fed up with the situation and ordered the APCs to pass over the railway tracks which they did and then drove up to the village. The two HVO soldiers were kind of stupid just standing there and guarding nothing, so they just packed up and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that the forces of your battalion entered from two different directions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eventually, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Eventually, into the village. Are there other things you can tell us about your observations in Stupni Do? You were telling us about 15 dead people, burnt people. The two burnt you found at the beginning are they included in the 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us something about the houses? Were they burnt or shot at or exploded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were exploded. It was just ruins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any building in the city left unhurt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any living person or living animal there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No living animal either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see many dead animals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were dead animals on the, let us say, fields, on the road, among the houses. Everything was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Killed, shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shot, burnt, sliced up throats, whatever you want to call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were no living creatures of any kind left in Stupni Do after the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to sum up for the court how many meetings you did have with the accused in this case, Ivica Rajic. How many times did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met him on six to eight occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Six to eight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even when Brigadier Henricsson was not with you, you met him even alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, always with him and to interpret for him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not for any other Commander or Officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You estimated six to eight ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: --- times. OK. Is there any question in your mind who was the Commanding Officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. Fine. I will ask you one concluding question pertaining to the question of the classification of the conflict, and that is: did you in your duties as an interpreter or in any other context make any observation to the involvement of the Croatian Army or the Croatian State in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean particularly in this case or in total?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you can take it generally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Like what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One example is, that has to be in spring time '93, we were in a village called Trevinja that is western Bosnia, Serb held, on a meeting with the Commander of that area on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were you accompanying then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Brigadier General Pellnas [sic]. They clearly stated that Croatian Army had gone in about 3 or 4 kilometres into Bosnia on the north eastern side of Dubrovnik in order to prevent the Serbs from shelling the Dubrovnik area. That was then confirmed by the Croatian Army Liaison Officer in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you experience this in your capacity of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any more examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next one is the latest, one of the latest offences made by the Croatian Army in it has to be summer '94 I think when they took a part of the area around Mostar and helped out the Bosnian troops in Bihac area. At that time the Croatian Army troop unit ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Army unit moved into a city village called Kuplitz. On the TV shots from those scenes you could see insignias of Croatian Army units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I recall from your statement that you had some experience to help some tanks be permitted to cross the border from Croatia into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a tank company from NORDBAT 2 who was supposed to go to our deployment area in Northern Bosnia which I was told by the UN had sold out by the UN as well. So we had take to them from Serbia down to via Hungary, Italy, down to Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All around Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All around ex Yugoslavia. They were a couple of months late, about four or five month late in the theatre. My task was to go down to Split, pick up this company of tanks together with the Mechanized Infantry company and guide them through Bosnia and make sure they got through checkpoints, up to the deployment area, area of responsibility for the battalion. I had in my hand a piece of paper signed by it was Deputy Minister of Interior in Croatia stating that the Croats should just leave these tanks alone and let them pass. However, then the UN forbid us to bring up the tanks to Bosnia. The explanation from Mr. Kirshee was that the Croats had made some problems with that. That is not true. I had the paper in my hand. So the Mechanized Infantry company came up to Tuzla and the tanks company had to stay on at Split for another couple, two months I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I went back up to -- that is all in January/February '94. Then I had to go back up to my unit to the Brigadier, and after two weeks I was sent to Mount Igman; one of the companies got the task to go to Mount Igman in Sarajevo and reinforce that when NATO this no fly zone, and no shelling, safe areas of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tell us now that has anything to do with the HVO or Croatian involvement in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. So we have no more examples from that kind of thing like HVO involvement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be Mostar in Spring '93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was present with Brigadier Pellnas [sic] in Mostar in '93, and there was some fighting going on. The fighting had just started in Mostar. We were present there and there was some contact between Zagreb to Mostar on HV side, on HVO side, to get them to start a ceasefire. They were more or less taking orders from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the meeting rooms when this took place. When they called they would say to Zagreb. I saw the number they were dialling, the area code, whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could hear the conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You understood the conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no question that it was in contact with Zagreb on these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I also met General Rosso.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rosso in Zagreb, the Ministry of Defence. If he is not fighting with them he has got nothing to do there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think I have one question. I listened to I think four instances or four examples that you gave us that you believe support your opinion that Croatia was involved in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct? I did have may hair cut about a few weeks ago! The one you mentioned was in, is it Trevinja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trevinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is that located in comparison to Vares? It is on the coast almost?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is inside of the coast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a good distance, is it not, from Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is down here, Trevinja, and you have Vares up here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any evidence that Croatia was involved in the area of the conflict that was going on in Vares and Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were insignias of some of the troops in the Vares area, was a Croatian Army unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that HV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw those insignias?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were inside Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were right in here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Vares? Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were right there, here, the middle of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that Vares you are pointing to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this that you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was during those events among Stupni Do and Vares, escalation later on, about a week later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them ever with Rajic in his presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe not as a unit. You could see one or two soldiers sitting in the dining room because the place of the whole meeting room was about 6 metres, 7 metres away from their dining room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the dining room in the Bobovac Headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would see HV soldiers, that is soldiers in Croatian uniform, in the Bobovac Headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time of the Stupni Do matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I do not know if I can say this, but to move around about 250 troops in and out through Vares, you cannot do that if you do not have the permission of Serbs on the other side. You cannot get the Serbs to agree upon that without Mladic knowing it and Mladic has in that case a deal with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is because to go from Vares and from Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am having difficulty -- to Stupni Do, you are saying that you would have to go through, you would have to have gone in October 1993 through Serbian controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you do not go through the Bosnian government controlled areas, and they will not let through 250 HVO troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously. So the only other way would be to go through Serbian, Bosnian-Serbian held territories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That could only have been with the permission of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are saying that that kind of permission would have to come from someone pretty high up in the Bosnian Serbian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mladic at least. Nobody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the troops then came from, the HVO troops, came from Vares or Kiseljak to Stupni Do, then they would have to have come through Bosnian-Serbian controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. It is your information that they did come from Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no other place to come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is that? There was no other ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From a transport location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From a transport point of view. But if you mean were the units actually came from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told that the units during the massacre in Stupni Do was HVO Kakanj. They came out of Kiseljak to Stupni Do. The unit originally came from Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Spell that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: K-A-K-A-N-J. That is just next to Vares up there. You have Vares there and Kakanj right there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they came from Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To Kiseljak and then from there where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from Vares to Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I talked to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A soldier, just major soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a BIH soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And also the girl that was raped and picked up by us on the search and rescue mission which I interrogated, she recognised some of those people from Kakanj. I then later on talked to the two soldiers that were guarding the mines under the railway bridge who also admitted it was HVO from Kakanj. That is the name of the unit, Kamar Kakanj. Then had deployed during the war whatsoever to Kiseljak especially for this action was brought to the Vares area of Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now these soldiers who came originally then would not have originally been part of the Bobovac Brigade, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were borrowed, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were brought in specially for one thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To do what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To wipe out Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You at one point went to the Bobovac Brigade officer, did you not, or headquarters and saw a number of soldiers there who were dressed and ready for combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain when that was approximately? What were they dressed like and did you draw any conclusions about whether they were combat ready or not based on their dress?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The normal uniform with HVO and Bosnian Army is they just put on anything they can get hold of. Camouflage or black is number one colours. When they get ready to do combats, they put on a small ribbon on the shoulder. It could be white, purple, any colour that just is the colour of the day for everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The colour of the day for everyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So they recognised each other because the two armies use the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they know each other. That helps ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: --- does not it? OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say if they start arming up a little bit more heavy, they got on this shoulder strap, they can see they are getting ready for combat. Some of them use -- the proper colour among Croats especially is the black uniform. I have seen it several places before around in the Krajina, outside Krajina, in Croatia, in Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this group of soldiers then at the Bobovac Brigade Headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would this have been before or after the attack on Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attack was ongoing when we got involved in it. We saw them at the first meeting up there in the Bobovac Brigade Headquarters. We saw them every time we go up there. Then finally when they were done on the third day we came up to look for Ivica Rajic. He was not there. We saw about five buses, four to five buses, fully packed with these soldiers getting ready to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they left the area did you hear them say anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were just shouting: "We are going to kill you. UNPROFOR sucks. NORDBAT sucks", and and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say anything about UNPROFOR being too late?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One guy said: "UNPROFOR is late as always. We have finished with our job, ha ha," and just started laughing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am looking at your statement, Mr. Ekenheim. Do you recall saying that Commander Rajic said that these were his troops in Stupni Do and he was in charge and he can guarantee that they will do nothing to harm the civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I guess that was in the second meeting with him when they made that statement; second or third meeting, something like that, the first night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stupni Do from listening to the other testimony was in a valley I gather, is that correct, like a little bowl or not? You tell me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stupni Do in comparison to Vares was on high grounds. Then the village was in a small valley that was, let us say, more level than higher ground than the rest of, let us say, Vares. So you could say it was in a valley, but it was higher ground than the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it on a main road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vares I gather was on a main road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to go through Vares to get to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any military significance to Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall saying in your statement that Commander Rajic said that he took Stupni Do because the Bosnian Army would launch an attack against Vares through there, so it had to be neutralized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say something about that earlier today? If so, I missed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. It was stated that the Bosnian Army was supposed to launch a major attack over Stupni Do to get Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in the first meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first meeting. OK.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have nothing further. Mr. Ostberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: One last question struck me. Can the words "Stupni Do" be translated into English? Does it mean something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a local dialect. It has to do with a finger, the knuckle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing to do with where it lies in the terrain or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. OK. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Sergeant Ekenheim. You are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: May I raise an issue?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We have two more witnesses: one is the photographer and the other is the Dutch Colonel Jan Koet who has been waiting to be examined today. I take it that you are not going to listen to two more witnesses today?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well, do you want to call Lieutenant Koet first?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No. Now we are planning to hear Pettersen, but if you are not going to hear Colonel Koet today he could be excused.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How long do you think you will need for Petty Officer Pettersen?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Madam President, I would estimate over half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then you can excuse Lieutenant Koet. We will just hear from Petty Officer Pettersen, but Judge Sidhwa reminds me for you to tell Lieutenant Colonel Koet to be available tomorrow at 2.30. That is when we plan to resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Of course. Petty Officer Pettersen, called.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Madam President, this witness will produce exhibits which are photographs which in the main the subject matter is very disturbing. I realise that there is a television output and there is a warning out on the screen, but I just thought I should bring it to the attention of the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What does the warning say? I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The warning says: "Some of the following images may be found to be disturbing".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may proceed. That is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed, it will be necessary for you to have your monitors switched on because these photographs will come up on the monitor as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: MR. CAYLEY (To the witness): Mr. Pettersen, thank you for coming to court today. You are Bernard John Pettersen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you are a Petty Officer in the Royal Navy of the United Kingdom is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you were interviewed by investigators from the Tribunal in June 1995 for two days and in August 1995 for two days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a little about your background. I think you joined the Royal Navy in 1976; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think in 1981 you attended the Joint Services Photographic Course; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which, in effect, trains you to be an officially trained military photographer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think in 1991 you attended the Advanced Photographic Course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes. I attended that course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that within your training you have done some forensic photography training, scenes of crime training and, indeed, in practice, you have been required to be involved in the photographic recording of Naval aviation crashes and scenes of crime records; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is also correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you have had operational experience with the Royal Navy in the Falkland zone from October 1984 to February 1985; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think in southwest Asia in December 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in August 19923 you were on temporary assignment to 845 Naval Air Squadron at Divelije Barracks in Split in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that this was part of the British contribution to the UN Protection Forces in the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think shortly after you arrived you were attached to the 1st Battalion, the Prince of Wales Own Royal Regiment of Yorkshire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you were, in fact, sent to them, as it were, to record their activities and their responsibilities in the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you were sent, were you not, to work for the Public Information Office making this photographic record of the battalion's activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this included visiting with members of the battalion, HVO units, Bosnian government units and, indeed, Bosnian Serb territories; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think during your time with the British battalion you frequently found yourself in difficult situations and you were often under direct fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think sometime in October 1993 you remember that you were required to travel from Vitez to Stupni Do to photograph an alleged massacre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you were accompanied by a rifle company from the British battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it is correct to state that you took over 300 photographs whilst you were in Stupni Do; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make a shot list of each of the negatives of the photographs which you took identifying exactly what that was a photograph of and where it was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. I actually logged each photograph and where it was on the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that when the Tribunal investigator came to visit you, you, in fact, made a more detailed shot list; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you, in fact, allocated an alphabetical list to each of the bodies that you photographed running from A to P; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should perhaps say human remains rather than bodies because in some cases, I think, they were not really identifiable as human remains; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The remains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think also when the Tribunal investigator came to record your statement you created a grid system which could be laid over a map or a plan of the village of Stupni Do which indicates from, as it were, the key on this grid system where each particular photograph was taken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Petty Officer Petterson, this is a very important part, you have not altered the prints or the negatives in any way; what we are going to see today is what you took at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The images you will see today and subsequently all those photographs are untouched or unaltered in any way, shape or form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Initially, is it correct in saying (and I emphasise initially) you did not actually move any of these bodies which you took photographs of in situ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, initially they were taken in situ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there were some problems entering Stupni Do, were there not? Could you explain to the court what happened as you got to I think it was a tunnel under a railway, was it not, that was the entrance to Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Just prior to that, your Honours, we approached Vares at night. We had been told that we might come under opposition, so we set off in the early morning at 3 o'clock. On approach to Vares we were actually stopped at a check point. There was a chain across the road and there was a guard and some mines on the road area. I was in a Landrover which was not armoured. We stopped at the checkpoint. We had armoured personnel carriers some 15 minutes behind us. My Major, the Major I was working with, actually got out and tried to talk to the soldiers to get our way through. A heated debate took place. I was back from that point at the time and actually took some photographs of the soldiers talking to the Major. After a long conversation, a Scandinavian vehicle came up and another argument took place with the Scandinavian officers and the soldiers at the checkpoint. After a lot of shouting and arguments, the chain was then removed, and I am not sure how the mines were removed, but we were allowed to proceed towards the village of Stupni Do. As we proceeded up the road, the entrance to Stupni Do was a tunnel area underneath a train track. We approached that in our Landrover, and the road was blocked by barbed wired and we were informed that there were possibly mines there. There was a sentry on top of the road block which it was clearly visible to see he had a weapon, a rifle of some sort. It was decided by the Major, Major Hunter, that it was too dangerous to actually proceed, and then the APCs were called for. We got into the APCs, which are armoured personal carriers, we got into them, and the Major decided it was still too dangerous to actually try to go under the tunnel, and he ordered the vehicles, the armoured personnel carriers, to go over the train tracks, and that is how we proceeded into the village. So, the armoured personnel carriers rode over the train tracks and carried on the path the other side of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
